## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

![](images/svg/margin_stack.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Agentic Machine Learning Systems Stack"}

*Agent stack focus for this chapter.*

_When is another token, candidate, check, or model call worth its cost?_

An agent that deliberates before acting pays latency and money for a better chance of success, whether it spends them on a longer derivation, more candidate patches, an extra check, or another model call. Each purchase answers a different question. More tokens re-examine what the prompt already holds, more candidates raise the chance that a good one sits somewhere in the pool, and only an executed check adds a fact the model did not have. None of them makes the returned answer correct, because a selector can return a plausible failure, and a search that optimizes against a flawed check finds the flaw faster than the fix. Deliberation is therefore a budgeted allocation problem with a stopping rule. The runtime decides where the next unit of work goes, how far a passing check can be trusted, and when to stop, abstain, or escalate instead of returning its best unverified guess. Every extra turn spent inside one decision lengthens the horizon, so that spending has to be bounded before the agent acts on anything.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare depth, breadth, and feedback by the information each adds, the tokens it consumes, and its critical path.
- Distinguish candidate availability from selected-output quality when evaluating voting, learned scoring, and task-specific checks.
- Calculate accepted-set precision from stated checker error rates and explain how adaptive search can change those assumptions.
- Represent a candidate plan as a dependency graph and identify which parts require revision after an observation changes.
- Design stopping rules that enforce resource ceilings without treating budget exhaustion as acceptance evidence.
- Evaluate competing deliberation policies under a common budget and deadline by pass probability, actual spend, and abstentions.

:::

## Limits of a Single Response {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-insufficient-response}

The repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) inspects the connection-pool implementation and receives a completed candidate patch. The invocation contract admits it as a candidate, yet the patch rests on an incomplete diagnosis. Client requests intermittently stall even after idle connections become available. Two distinct failure modes can produce this symptom: an aggressive timeout configuration that aborts prematurely, or a lost notification when a worker thread returns a connection to the pool. When prompted, the language model proposes extending the timeout. That change offers a plausible workaround, but it provides no evidence that the timeout caused the stalls. Deploying such a patch immediately risks masking the latency tail while leaving the concurrency defect intact.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_h.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the Horizon axis highlighted."}

*Deliberation extends the horizon with extra model turns and checks inside one decision, and hard ceilings bound that spend.*
:::

Before committing to an edit, the agent runtime can invest computational work in several distinct ways. It can grant the model a longer derivation budget to trace the lock acquisition and release sequence in detail; it can sample diverse candidate patches that modify different components of the pooling logic; or it can execute a targeted harness to record whether a waiting thread actually receives the condition variable notification. Each strategy purchases a different kind of evidence. Extended internal reasoning can expose subtle logical flaws in the source text. Sampling across temperature or prompt variations can surface novel implementations that a greedy single pass misses. An instrumented test, by contrast, delivers empirical observations of runtime state, which reveal dynamic interactions that static token generation alone cannot establish.

This division marks the operational boundary between internal computation and empirical observation. Additional model computation re-evaluates information already present in the prompt context. Within a single generation, a model can backtrack and revise an earlier analytical misstep even as the previous tokens remain frozen in its context prefix. However, pure computation cannot generate new empirical facts. Only an executed test reports how the running process behaves, and its conclusions remain strictly bounded by the specific conditions and interleavings that the test harness exercised.

Suppose the targeted test forces an interleaving where a worker thread waits while another returns a connection. The execution trace reveals that the connection successfully enters the pool, yet the waiting worker remains blocked past the notification point. This empirical finding rules out the timeout hypothesis immediately and directs the agent toward the synchronization path. The agent can then synthesize a patch that repairs the signaling logic and verify it against the failing reproducer. Passing a targeted reproducer, however, does not constitute full task acceptance; narrow tests can overlook edge cases, and neither an unverified hypothesis nor an isolated micro-test provides sufficient confidence to ship code to production. The two paths part ways before any file changes (@fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree). Acting on the first guess hides the symptom and keeps the defect, whereas checking first spends one short test to learn which hypothesis survives.

::: {#fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It**: Both paths start from the same connection-pool failure. On the left, generation builds on the timeout explanation without any observation that separates it from a missed notification, so the patch can hide the symptom while the defect remains. On the right, a targeted test orders a waiting worker and a returning connection, and its observation contradicts the timeout explanation before any edit. The revised candidate passes the reproducer, which still falls short of task acceptance." fig-alt="Two lanes below a box reading observed failure, request waits after a connection frees. The left lane, labeled commit first, holds H1 timeout too short with H2 missed notification drawn faded and dashed, then generate on H1 with no new evidence, then a timeout patch applied unchecked, ending in a red box reading symptom masked, notification defect remains. The right lane, labeled check first, holds both H1 and H2, then an amber targeted test observing the waiter still blocked after return, then the hypotheses again with H1 struck through and marked contradicted, then a notify on return patch, the revised candidate from H2, ending in a green box reading reproducer passes, acceptance still pending. A dashed horizontal line labeled first edit crosses both lanes: the left lane reaches it with no check, the right lane only after the test."}
![](images/svg/diagnostic_tree.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-probe-allocation
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PROBE AND GENERATION ALLOWANCES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-probe-versus-generation.
# │ Goal: Compare a short diagnostic operation with an output allowance.
# │ Show: Generation time and output charge, distinct from probe duration.
# │ How: Reuse the registry weight-read allowance from Foundation Model;
# │      exclude prefill, queueing, transport, and probe setup overhead.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8

class ProbeAllocation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    answer_tokens = 1_024  # hypothetical output length
    probe_time = 0.040 * second  # hypothetical already-prepared test duration
    output_price = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical dollars per output token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    answer_time = answer_tokens * token_time
    answer_cost = answer_tokens * output_price
    time_ratio = answer_time / probe_time

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(answer_time > probe_time > 0 * second, "Positive scenario durations")
    check(answer_cost > 0 * USD, "Output has a positive scenario charge")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    answer_tokens_str = fmt_int(answer_tokens)
    probe_time_str = fmt_time(probe_time, unit="ms", precision=0)
    token_time_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit="ms", precision=2)
    answer_time_str = fmt_time(answer_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    answer_cost_str = fmt_usd(answer_cost, precision=5)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_price * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    time_mult_str = fmt_multiple(time_ratio, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-03-probe-versus-generation .callout-notebook title="A probe vs. a longer answer"}

**Problem**: A prepared diagnostic test takes `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str`. A proposed explanation contains `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str` output tokens. How long does the explanation take to generate relative to the test?

**Variables**: The illustrative per-token generation time from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate is `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str`, derived from memory-bandwidth limits rather than a measured production service rate. The hypothetical output pricing is `{python} ProbeAllocation.output_price_str` per million tokens. Prompt processing, queueing, transport, test preparation, and the downstream model call that reads the test observation are excluded.

**Math**: Generating `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str` tokens at `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` per token requires `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str` and incurs `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_cost_str` in token charges. Dividing this generation latency by the `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str` test run yields a factor of `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: When the unresolved question concerns dynamic program behavior, the probe settles it `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str` faster than the model can generate a speculative explanation of it, and only the probe's answer is an observation. Running a test is preferable whenever its preparation and execution time remain below the explanation's `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str` and its outcome decisively discriminates between competing failure modes. Conversely, an inconclusive test that does not discriminate the competing hypotheses provides no diagnostic gain regardless of its speed. Failure to reproduce can still supply negative evidence when the test's sensitivity to the suspected fault is known. A well-designed runtime allocates work to whichever operation most efficiently eliminates the primary source of uncertainty.

:::

The probe, and the decision to revise the patch on its evidence, both happened outside any single model call. The invocation contract of the previous chapter ends at one prompt and one candidate, accompanied only by metadata indicating whether generation reached a stop token or an output limit. That interface cannot evaluate whether allocating the next second of latency or fraction of a cent toward extended reasoning, candidate sampling, or runtime probing would yield a higher-quality fix. An API response signaling completion merely confirms that generation finished, not that the proposed patch resolves the underlying defect. **Test-time compute**\index{Test-time compute!definition} is all the system work orchestrated around the model call, with model weights held fixed, to explore, evaluate, and verify candidates before committing to an action. An effective agentic architecture requires a principled runtime policy to govern this expenditure: establishing hard ceilings on latency and financial cost, routing compute across reasoning and validation tools, and terminating search cleanly without conflating an exhausted resource quota with a verified solution.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The bounded single-invocation model contract is established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract.
:::

Each part of that policy raises the next question. The runtime first chooses how to spend extra work across reasoning depth, candidate breadth, and empirical feedback (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-computation-allocation). Breadth produces a pool, so the runtime must then pick from it without being fooled by a plausible failure (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity), and picking well depends on how far a passing check can be trusted (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification). When a check refutes a premise partway through a plan, the runtime should regenerate only what depended on it (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision). Candidates and revisions together form a search whose spending must be tracked, reserved, and stopped (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search), and the complete policy is finally judged against its alternatives under one budget and one deadline (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-strategy-design).

## Three Compute Allocation Axes {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-computation-allocation}

When diagnosing and fixing a concurrency bug in a connection pool, an agent system can unroll an exhaustive step-by-step derivation, sample several candidate patches in parallel, or iterate through an edit–test–revise loop. While all three strategies can consume an identical token allowance, they impose fundamentally different execution topologies. A detailed derivation must generate tokens sequentially along a single causal chain. Independent candidate patches can execute concurrently across accelerator hardware. An iterative revision cycle that incorporates test results must pause generation until diagnostic execution finishes. These structural dependencies dictate which operations lie on the critical latency path and how much state the serving infrastructure must retain in memory.

**Depth**\index{Depth axis!definition} extends sequential computation within a single candidate, **breadth**\index{Breadth axis!definition} explores multiple candidate paths concurrently, and **feedback**\index{Feedback axis!definition} incorporates environment observations into subsequent revisions. A **test-time deliberation rollout**\index{Test-time deliberation rollout!definition}\index{Deliberation|see{Test-time deliberation rollout}} represents one bounded candidate-generation path, potentially interleaving verification checks and observation-conditioned revisions; the term borrows from game search, where a rollout plays one line of moves forward to its end. Depth lengthens a rollout, breadth runs several, and feedback inserts checks between a rollout's turns. An allocation policy can compose these axes. It might, for example, generate several candidate patches in parallel, run automated regression suites against each, and extend only the most promising candidate with step-by-step reasoning. Throughout this process, model weights remain frozen; every axis draws against a shared test-time allowance.

::: {#dfn-vol3-test-time-compute-budget .callout-definition title="Test-time compute budget"}

***Test-time compute budget***\index{Test-time compute budget!definition} is the per-decision allowance of processed prompt tokens, generated tokens, model invocations, verification checks, and elapsed wall-clock time that a runtime may expend, with model weights fixed, before it must select a candidate, abstain, or escalate to a human operator.

1.  **Significance**: The budget sets the attempt cost in the effective cost per accepted task, $\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). Additional deliberation reduces cost per accepted task when it increases the acceptance rate $\AcceptanceProbability$ proportionally faster than it increases the expected attempt cost. A higher cost per accepted task can still be justified when it buys the required acceptance rate within the deadline (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-operating-point).
2.  **Distinction**: Training compute amortizes weight optimization once across all future tasks. Test-time compute recurs on every decision, where an internal reasoning allowance is merely one control surface alongside external tool invocations and verification checks.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the maximum allocation ceiling as the expected spend, or treating an exhausted budget as evidence that the best remaining candidate is acceptable.

:::

What separates the three axes is their dependency structure (@fig-vol3-allocation-axes). Depth extends a single candidate through multi-step reasoning, breadth fans out to sampled candidates that converge on a selector, and feedback routes a candidate through a sandboxed check whose observation conditions the revision.

::: {#fig-vol3-allocation-axes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Three compute allocation topologies**: Depth extends one candidate; breadth exposes separate sampled candidate paths followed by selection; feedback makes a later candidate depend on an observed check result. The arrows show dependencies, not guaranteed latency, cost, or correctness." fig-alt="Three panels labeled Depth, Breadth, and Feedback. Depth connects an input through a single chain of four reasoning segments to a candidate. Breadth fans an input out to three separate two-segment sample paths, bracketed as sampled paths, that converge on a selector, which outputs a candidate. Feedback sends a candidate into a dashed sandbox region containing a check, which produces an observation; a revised candidate receives one arrow from the observation and one from the original candidate."}
![](images/svg/three_compute_allocation_axes.svg)
:::

### Sequential extension along the depth axis {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-depth-axis}

Depth allows an autoregressive model to unroll intermediate reasoning tokens before emitting its final decision or artifact, generalizing early scratchpad techniques and chain-of-thought prompting [@nye2021show; @wei2022cot]. In the connection-pool scenario, these intermediate tokens might systematically trace thread interleavings: acquiring the pool mutex, detecting leaked socket descriptors, and signaling waiter condition variables. Because autoregressive generation conditions on all prior tokens, later decoding steps can inspect earlier derivations, detect flawed assumptions, and alter course before outputting code. This reasoning advantage arises entirely from executing additional forward passes over the prompt context rather than modifying the underlying network weights.

From a systems perspective, generation remains strictly autoregressive. Extending a single generation path serializes the computation. Because transformer decoding at small batch sizes is memory-bandwidth bound, step latency is governed by the time required to stream all model parameters from high-bandwidth memory into processor caches (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}). Consequently, wall-clock generation time scales approximately linearly with the number of generated tokens under a fixed serving configuration. A lengthy reasoning trace demonstrates only that the accelerator performed more computation, not that the proposed code compiles or executes correctly. The runtime must also leave enough output budget for the final usable artifact. A derivation that exhausts the budget mid-generation returns a truncated response, which the invocation contract quarantines like any other incomplete call rather than treating it as a candidate.

### Parallel sampling along the breadth axis {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-breadth-axis}

Breadth allocates test-time compute across alternative candidate paths. Instead of extending one trajectory, the runtime requests multiple candidate patches from the same source excerpt and task specification, using stochastic decoding controls. Conditional on a fixed prompt and independent random seeds, these samples are statistically independent draws from the model's output distribution. However, they remain bounded by the model's underlying knowledge: if the model assigns negligible probability mass to a correct thread-notification pattern, every independent sample may reproduce the same missing broadcast. Independent draws can easily fail in identical ways.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Temperature, top-$\Glyph{k}$, and nucleus sampling controls are established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-sampling-controls.
:::

Because parallel candidates share no sequential dependencies, breadth exposes fine-grained concurrency. On modern accelerator hardware, this concurrency comes at minimal latency cost. Under memory-bandwidth-bound decoding (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}), a batch of $\CandidatePoolSize$ concurrent candidate streams reads the model weights once per step for all $\CandidatePoolSize$ tokens. Spending an allocation of $\CandidatePoolSize \times \OutputLength$ tokens sequentially along the depth axis multiplies the generation latency by roughly $\CandidatePoolSize$. In contrast, generating $\CandidatePoolSize$ concurrent candidates of length $\OutputLength$ in parallel keeps total generation time near the duration of the longest candidate, $\max_n \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_n)$. This latency benefit holds as long as the concurrent batch remains memory-bandwidth bound and fits within accelerator memory.

Accelerator memory is where breadth extracts its price. Each active generation stream must maintain its own key-value (KV) cache for the tokens it generates. When the serving system implements prefix sharing, the $\SequenceLength$-token prompt is stored once in memory, and the peak KV cache demand scales as

$$
\BreadthPeakKvCacheMemory \propto \SequenceLength + \sum_{n=1}^{\CandidatePoolSize} \OutputLength_n
$$

Without shared prefix caching, the serving engine stores $\CandidatePoolSize$ redundant copies of the prompt's KV tensors, causing memory demand to scale as $\CandidatePoolSize \SequenceLength + \sum_n \OutputLength_n$. When aggregate KV cache allocations exceed hardware capacity, the serving engine must partition candidates into sequential execution waves. Once forced into waves, breadth latency degrades from the duration of the single longest candidate toward the sum of all candidates, while memory thrashing and queueing delays increase individual token latencies. Whether identical prompt prefixes share physical memory or receive provider billing discounts depends on the serving engine's implementation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Block sharing, which stores a common prompt's KV state once for every candidate that branches from it, is developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-cow-prefix-sharing.
:::

Breadth also shifts the operational burden downstream: generating a wide pool of candidates pays off only if the system can accurately select the best option or synthesize their differences. A candidate pool containing an optimal patch provides no value without an effective selector. In a study of repeated sampling, @brown2024monkeys showed that while the probability of at least one candidate being correct (pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$) continued to rise across four orders of magnitude of samples, practical selection heuristics such as majority voting and learned reward models (scorers trained to predict whether a candidate is correct, examined in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-outcome-step-evidence) plateaued after several hundred samples. Candidate selection is therefore an active consumer of compute and verification budget rather than an incidental final step.

### Observation-conditioned revision along the feedback axis {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-feedback-axis}

The feedback axis incorporates external observations into subsequent model requests. Rather than relying solely on frozen weights and static inputs, the repair agent generates a candidate patch, the runtime executes a bounded test suite, and the subsequent model invocation receives concrete diagnostics, such as a stack trace from a deadlocked worker thread. These empirical observations constrain subsequent candidate generation far more effectively than prompting the model to re-examine the original prompt in isolation [@shinn2023reflexion].

Verification checks yield structured outcomes: failure, success, or inconclusive execution (such as a test timeout). A failure trace pinpoints specific regression bugs or unmet invariants; a passing test confirms that the code satisfies the exercised assertions under tested conditions; and final acceptance remains a distinct policy gate. Executing diagnostics constitutes an active external action. It consumes CPU and memory resources, runs within sandboxed security boundaries, and incurs wall-clock latency even when performed purely for internal deliberation.

Each feedback round is also one more turn of the horizon $\TurnHorizon$, which ties this axis to horizon compounding (@eq-vol3-horizon-compounding). Unchecked turns compound error as $(1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}$, and the introduction showed (notebook \ref{nbk-01-horizon-compounding}) that a check which rejects a bad step and retries it resets that compounding. Feedback is the one axis that places such a check inside every turn, so it can lengthen a deliberation without the unchecked compounding its extra turns would otherwise carry, to the extent that its checks deserve trust (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification).

Feedback introduces strict serialization: a revision cannot begin until the preceding verification check completes and returns its observation payload. Furthermore, context policies that append prior candidates and diagnostic outputs cause input token counts to expand across successive turns. For an initial prompt length $\BasePromptLength$, candidate lengths $\OutputLength_j$, and observation lengths $\lvert \TrajectoryObservation_j\rvert$, an append-only policy yields an input length at turn $\TurnIndex$ of

$$\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)} = \BasePromptLength + \sum_{j=1}^{\TurnIndex-1}(\OutputLength_j + \lvert \TrajectoryObservation_j\rvert)$$

This is the append-only growth that @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend priced across a whole trajectory, now confined to one decision, and it inflates prompt prefill latency, accelerator memory usage, and token billing on every round. Although context-compaction techniques can summarize earlier attempts or drop obsolete diagnostic traces, the allocation policy must account for the full token volume dispatched to the model API.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Context-compaction methods and their scheduling within the request budget are developed in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction.
:::

### The three axes under one output ceiling {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-common-output-ceiling}

Runtimes schedule these three allocation axes against four resource dimensions: input and output token counts, critical-path wall-clock latency, peak retained accelerator state, and external information acquisition. Let $\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength)$ be the time required to ingest an $\SequenceLength$-token prompt, $\PerTokenDecodeTime$ the per-token decoding step time, $\DecodeInterval(\OutputLength)$ the total generation time for $\OutputLength$ tokens, and $\FeedbackCheckDuration$ the duration of the external check in feedback round $\TurnIndex$, which is also the turn index of the trajectory. With $\ExtendedDepthLength$ tokens of extended depth, $\CandidatePoolSize$ breadth candidates executed concurrently, and $\TurnHorizon$ feedback turns, the latency dimension decomposes into three critical paths:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\DepthCriticalPathLatency &\approx \PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) + \ExtendedDepthLength\,\PerTokenDecodeTime,\\
\BreadthCriticalPathLatency &\approx \PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) + \max_{n} \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_n),\\
\FeedbackCriticalPathLatency &\approx \sum_{t=1}^{\TurnHorizon}\bigl(\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}) + \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_t) + {\FeedbackCheckDuration}_{\TurnIndex}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path}

The critical path for breadth assumes the serving infrastructure maintains sufficient memory and execution capacity to decode all $\CandidatePoolSize$ streams concurrently at an unchanged step time. When capacity saturates, decoding falls back into serialized waves, shifting the critical path toward the sum across candidate streams. In contrast, the feedback expression grows along two distinct dimensions: sequential check durations $\FeedbackCheckDuration$ and lengthening prompt prefill times $\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)})$ caused by context accumulation. The equation covers only latency. @Tbl-vol3-allocation-model sets those critical paths beside the other three dimensions, the tokens processed, the peak model state retained, and the external information acquired.

| **Axis** | **Tokens processed**                                                                                        | **Critical path**                  | **Peak retained model state**                                                                  | **New information**                      |
|:---------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Depth    | $\SequenceLength + \ExtendedDepthLength$                                                                    | One dependent sequence             | One context of $\SequenceLength + \ExtendedDepthLength$ tokens                                 | None beyond the request and weights      |
| Breadth  | $\SequenceLength + \sum_n \OutputLength_n$ (prompt shared)                                                  | Longest candidate, given capacity  | $\CandidatePoolSize$ contexts, $\SequenceLength + \sum_n \OutputLength_n$ tokens if shared     | Sampling variation over the same request |
| Feedback | $\sum_{t}(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)} + \OutputLength_t)$, with $\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}$ growing | Sum of turns, including each check | One active context of $\SequenceLength^{(\TurnHorizon)} + \OutputLength_{\TurnHorizon}$ tokens | Observations from executed checks        |

: **Resource model of the three allocation axes**: Symbolic accounting of processed tokens, critical path, retained model state, and information source. Concurrency and prefix sharing are capacity and implementation assumptions, not properties of the axis. {#tbl-vol3-allocation-model tbl-colwidths="[11,23,22,25,19]"}

Among the three topologies, only feedback admits external information absent from the model weights and prompt. The code below models these expressions for the connection-pool repair under a fixed output budget of 4,096 tokens, isolating how identical output ceilings generate starkly different latency profiles and monetary bills.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-allocation-axes
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMMON OUTPUT CEILING, DIFFERENT EXECUTION TOPOLOGIES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-matched-budget-axes.
# │ Goal: Separate output ceilings, actual spend, and dependent elapsed time.
# │ Show: Input/output counts, hypothetical bills, and generation/check time.
# │ How: Hold model allowance fixed; stipulate four concurrent breadth streams.
# │      Feedback appends each prior candidate and report; no cache discounts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8

class AllocationAxes:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    prompt = 4_096  # hypothetical fully serialized initial input tokens
    ceiling = 4_096  # common total generated-token ceiling
    candidates = 4  # breadth concurrency and candidate count
    candidate_tokens = 1_024  # hypothetical generated length per short candidate
    rounds = 3  # hypothetical feedback rounds actually used
    report = 340  # tokens appended per complete observation
    check_time = 1.5 * second  # hypothetical duration per feedback check
    price_in = 3 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-input-token price
    price_out = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-output-token price

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    depth_input = prompt
    depth_output = ceiling
    breadth_input = candidates * prompt
    breadth_output = candidates * candidate_tokens
    feedback_input = rounds * prompt + (candidate_tokens + report) * rounds * (rounds - 1) // 2
    feedback_output = rounds * candidate_tokens
    depth_time = depth_output * token_time
    breadth_time = candidate_tokens * token_time
    feedback_time = rounds * (candidate_tokens * token_time + check_time)
    depth_cost = depth_input * price_in + depth_output * price_out
    breadth_cost = breadth_input * price_in + breadth_output * price_out
    feedback_cost = feedback_input * price_in + feedback_output * price_out
    path_ratio = (depth_time / breadth_time).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    bill_ratio = (breadth_cost / depth_cost).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    breadth_premium = breadth_input - depth_input  # (N - 1) P re-read prompt tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(depth_output == breadth_output == ceiling, "Depth and breadth exhaust ceiling")
    check(feedback_output < ceiling, "Feedback uses less than the output ceiling")
    check(feedback_input == 16_380, "Append-only feedback input accounting")
    check(depth_time > feedback_time > breadth_time, "Scenario critical-path ordering")
    check(breadth_premium == (candidates - 1) * prompt, "Breadth premium is the re-read prompt")
    check(bill_ratio > 1 and path_ratio > 1, "Breadth buys path length with bill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    ceiling_str = fmt_int(ceiling)
    candidates_str = fmt_int(candidates)
    candidate_tokens_str = fmt_int(candidate_tokens)
    rounds_str = fmt_int(rounds)
    report_str = fmt_int(report)
    check_time_str = fmt_time(check_time, unit="s", precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    depth_input_str = fmt_int(depth_input)
    depth_output_str = fmt_int(depth_output)
    breadth_input_str = fmt_int(breadth_input)
    breadth_output_str = fmt_int(breadth_output)
    feedback_input_str = fmt_int(feedback_input)
    feedback_output_str = fmt_int(feedback_output)
    depth_time_str = fmt_time(depth_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    breadth_time_str = fmt_time(breadth_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    feedback_time_str = fmt_time(feedback_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    depth_cost_str = fmt_usd(depth_cost, precision=5)
    breadth_cost_str = fmt_usd(breadth_cost, precision=5)
    feedback_cost_str = fmt_usd(feedback_cost, precision=5)
    path_mult_str = fmt_multiple(path_ratio, precision=0)
    bill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bill_ratio, precision=1)
    breadth_premium_str = fmt_int(breadth_premium)
```

::: {#nbk-03-matched-budget-axes .callout-notebook title="One decision, three allocations"}

**Problem**: A repair request starts with `{python} AllocationAxes.prompt_str` input tokens and a common ceiling of `{python} AllocationAxes.ceiling_str` generated tokens. How do depth, breadth, and feedback spend that allowance?

**Variables**: Reuse the illustrative per-token generation time from the preceding example. Breadth has capacity for `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` concurrent streams at that same rate. Each short candidate uses `{python} AllocationAxes.candidate_tokens_str` generated tokens. Feedback uses `{python} AllocationAxes.rounds_str` turns, each followed by a `{python} AllocationAxes.check_time_str` check returning `{python} AllocationAxes.report_str` tokens. Later feedback requests append earlier candidates and reports. Hypothetical prices are `{python} AllocationAxes.price_in_str` per million input tokens and `{python} AllocationAxes.price_out_str` per million output tokens, without cache discounts, so each breadth stream is billed for its own copy of the prompt (unlike the shared-prefix row of @tbl-vol3-allocation-model). Generation times omit prefill, queueing, and transport; the feedback time additionally includes its checks. The bill counts model tokens only, and @tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs tallies each allocation's tokens, time, and bill side by side.

| Allocation |                                 Input tokens |                                 Output tokens |              Generation and included checks |                            Model-token bill |
|:-----------|---------------------------------------------:|----------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|
| Depth      |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_input_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_output_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_time_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_cost_str` |
| Breadth    |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_input_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_output_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_time_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_cost_str` |
| Feedback   | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_input_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_output_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_time_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_cost_str` |
: **Allocation accounting under a common output ceiling**: Equal ceilings produce unequal spend. Allowances omit prefill, queueing, selection, and tool charges. {#tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs}

**Math**: In @tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs, depth generates all `{python} AllocationAxes.ceiling_str` tokens along a single path. Breadth generates `{python} AllocationAxes.candidate_tokens_str` tokens on each of `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` concurrent paths, shortening the critical path by `{python} AllocationAxes.path_mult_str`. However, reading the prompt `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` times across unshared streams adds `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_premium_str` input tokens, multiplying its billing cost to `{python} AllocationAxes.bill_mult_str` that of depth. Feedback accumulates input context over $\TurnHorizon$ turns according to $\TurnHorizon\,\BasePromptLength + (\OutputLength + \lvert \TrajectoryObservation\rvert)\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)/2$, reaching `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_input_str` tokens at $\TurnHorizon =$ `{python} AllocationAxes.rounds_str` because each successive round re-reads all prior candidates and observation reports.

**Systems insight**: Breadth trades monetary cost for reduced wall-clock latency, where the entire billing premium stems from the $(\CandidatePoolSize-1)\SequenceLength$ re-read prompt tokens. The key governing lever is the ratio of prompt length to generated output: a large repository context makes breadth's financial overhead scale aggressively with both $\CandidatePoolSize$ and $\SequenceLength$, whereas a short prompt or a shared prefix cache eliminates most of this penalty. Feedback achieves an intermediate balance between latency and billing cost while remaining the only topology capable of acquiring empirical ground truth. Because this resource accounting excludes solution success rates, it models infrastructural cost rather than output quality.

:::

### Internal budgets and external orchestration {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-latent-vs-scaffold}

Production systems operate across two distinct control planes: internal model deliberation and external workflow orchestration. A model service may expose an internal reasoning budget, while the runtime independently governs how many calls to dispatch, which tool checks to invoke, and what context to supply in subsequent requests. These represent different control surfaces. An internal budget governs the reasoning depth permitted within a single model invocation; external orchestration directs breadth across candidate branches, schedules sandboxed verification runs, and constructs revised prompts. Because commercial APIs often hide or redact intermediate reasoning traces, the runtime cannot evaluate computational effort by inspecting output text lengths. Instead, it must rely on explicit token usage headers and invocation status codes to enforce quotas and track system cost.

### Reasoning models and generation allowances {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-reasoning-models}

**Reasoning models**\index{Reasoning model!definition} undergo reinforcement learning on tasks with objective, verifiable outcomes, such as formal mathematics, logic puzzles, and unit-tested codebases. Through this training, they learn to produce extended intermediate scratchpads that propose solutions, verify intermediate steps, and backtrack within a single generation pass [@openai2024o1; @deepseekai2025deepseekr1]. For system designers, this architecture introduces three core operational implications:

1.  *Token metering*: Reasoning tokens are standard autoregressive output tokens. They consume accelerator compute, populate the KV cache, and incur standard decoding charges, regardless of whether the user interface displays them or redacts them behind summary metadata.
2.  *Dynamic depth control*: A reasoning-budget parameter\index{Reasoning budget} transforms sequential depth from a static model property into a dynamic, per-request runtime allocation. The orchestration layer can calibrate this knob on a per-task basis.
3.  *Knowledge boundaries*: Internal reasoning operates strictly over the supplied prompt and static network weights. An extended trace can verify arithmetic or check internal logic consistency, but it cannot observe external execution behavior. It cannot determine whether a proposed patch resolves a connection leak without running an actual test suite.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, the training that produces reasoning models, is developed in @sec-vol3-rlvr.
:::

Because models trained with verifiable rewards use generation allowances differently than instruction-tuned models (models adapted to follow example instructions and responses), budget calibration is highly model-dependent. Furthermore, when internal reasoning traces remain hidden, the runtime can inspect only its own external invocation telemetry and verification results. These records guide the optimization of orchestration policies rather than providing formal guarantees of candidate correctness.

Treating depth as a per-call budget allows the runtime to allocate tokens dynamically across tasks. The core engineering objective is determining what each compute allocation topology yields across tasks of varying intrinsic difficulty.

::: {#exmp-03-compute-optimal-allocation .callout-example title="Compute-optimal test-time allocation"}

**Scenario**: @snell2024scaling evaluated strategies for spending a fixed test-time compute budget across reasoning benchmarks, comparing sequential revision of a single candidate against parallel breadth sampling and search guided by learned process verifiers (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification). The study partitioned benchmark problems into difficulty tiers based on the base model's zero-shot success rate.

**Diagnosis**: On simpler problems, sequential revision used the compute budget most effectively, refining minor errors without the overhead of parallel sampling. On moderately difficult problems, hybrid strategies combining parallel exploration with guided search achieved higher accuracy. On the hardest problems, however, scaling test-time compute yielded diminishing returns across all allocation axes. When evaluated at matched total FLOPs, a compute-optimal test-time allocation enabled a smaller model to outperform a model 14 times larger, provided the smaller model possessed a nonzero base success rate. When base success hovered near zero, allocating FLOPs to a larger, more capable base model proved far more effective than exhausting tokens on parallel rollouts.

**Systems lesson**: With the supplied information held fixed, additional reasoning and sampling can elicit nonzero baseline capabilities but cannot acquire absent environmental facts. Feedback can supply new observations to the next call, whose value still depends on the model's ability to use them and the check's coverage. Runtimes should dynamically route compute budgets by estimated task difficulty: allocate modest budgets or single candidates to straightforward tasks, deploy parallel search to moderately complex tasks, and escalate near-zero confidence requests directly to larger models or human supervisors rather than wasting tokens on unguided sampling.

:::

Because an execution engine cannot directly observe intrinsic task difficulty a priori, it must approximate difficulty using low-latency, low-cost heuristics before committing an expensive deliberation budget. Practical heuristics include consensus among two or three low-temperature pilot samples, the output of fast static analysis linters, and historical error rates across similar task classes. When pilot signals demonstrate high consensus or pass static checks cleanly, the runtime allocates a minimal token budget to a single candidate. When pilot samples diverge or linters flag structural ambiguities, the scheduler escalates the request to a broader search or an iterative feedback loop. If a decision remains unresolved after exhausting a bounded budget ceiling, the runtime halts deliberation and escalates to a human operator rather than burning additional tokens on low-probability convergence. Each routing heuristic acts as a predictive classifier whose precision and recall must be empirically validated against held-out task distributions.

In production agent workflows, internal reasoning depth and external search breadth naturally compose. A single deliberation rollout may use enough depth to generate a structurally coherent, well-reasoned code patch; the runtime then samples several such reasoned candidates across the breadth axis and filters them through an automated test harness along the feedback axis. The composition must still be tuned to real system bottlenecks. Slow tool execution inflates feedback latency along the critical path, whereas imprecise test suites diminish the informational value of each feedback observation.

The checks that make this composition work matter beyond inference. The validation checks a runtime uses to accept candidates at test time are the same kind of check that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards turns into a training reward. An edge case, false pass, or specification gap in a test-time acceptance check therefore costs one bad selection at inference, but once the check becomes a reward, training searches for that gap on every update.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How an acceptance check becomes a training reward, and how its gaps are exploited during training, is developed in @sec-vol3-rlvr-rewards.
:::

::: {#chk-03-compute-allocation-axes .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing an allocation"}

- [ ] **Information**: For the connection-pool repair, which axis can separate a short timeout from a missed notification, and why can the other two not?
- [ ] **Concurrency**: If the service admits only one candidate at a time, how long does the notebook's breadth allocation take to generate, and which allocation then has the shortest path?
- [ ] **Breadth premium**: How many extra input tokens does `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str`-way breadth read compared with depth for a `{python} AllocationAxes.prompt_str`-token prompt, and what happens to that premium when the repository context grows eightfold?
- [ ] **Evidence**: If a revised patch passes a targeted test, what additional information determines whether the task may stop?

:::

Allocating compute across depth, breadth, and feedback defines where extra computation is spent, but generation alone does not determine which candidate should survive. Even an allocation that discovers a correct repair fails if downstream selection favors a plausible incorrect alternative. The remaining challenge is candidate evaluation: comparing competing proposals while accounting for the costs, latencies, and blind spots of the verification mechanisms that judge them.

## Candidate Selection {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity}

Generating a broad candidate pool gives an agent a portfolio of proposals, but breadth alone does not solve a task. In a connection-pool repair task, for example, one candidate might lengthen an acquisition timeout, another might inject exponential retries, and a third might alter how the connection-return path notifies waiting threads. The runtime must determine which proposal, if any, carries sufficient supporting evidence to return, and evaluating that evidence consumes execution time and tokens from the same deliberation budget that generated the candidates.

Two distinct requirements separate generation from selection: whether the candidate pool contains at least one solution that satisfies the task requirements, and whether the selector can identify that valid solution without mistakenly accepting an unsuitable one. A generation policy can flood the pool with candidate solutions without making selection any easier. Conversely, a more discerning selector can dramatically raise the reliability of the system without sampling a single extra candidate.

### Useful variation among candidates {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-variation}

Syntactic variation does not guarantee algorithmic diversity. Renaming local variables, reformatting comments, or rewriting an iteration loop can produce completely distinct token sequences while leaving a broken synchronization bug completely untouched. For our repair task, candidate alternatives provide practical value only when they explore distinct hypotheses or failure modes that downstream checks can actually differentiate. Adjusting thread notification logic vs. extending a timeout explores two different failure hypotheses; generating several slightly reworded explanations for the same timeout adjustment simply wastes verification cycles.

This failure mode is distinct from statistical dependence. When the task, prompt, base model, and sampling policy remain fixed, separate generation passes driven by independent random seeds are genuinely independent and identically distributed (IID). However, if the model concentrates nearly all its probability mass on timeout adjustments, independent sampling predictably floods the pool with variations of that single change.

Across a heterogeneous production workload, common model limitations become even more pronounced. A model typically solves standard, well-represented patterns reliably while failing consistently on obscure edge cases. Consequently, repeated attempts on a difficult task fail together far more frequently than an aggregate benchmark pass rate would imply. While individual samples on a single fixed task may be conditionally independent, treating attempts across a mixed workload as draws with one common success probability obscures this correlation. Feedback-conditioned generation further alters the distribution: when the runtime feeds execution errors back into subsequent prompts, later candidates become explicitly dependent on what earlier checks revealed.

A runtime can encourage diversity by adjusting sampling parameters or prompting the model to explore distinct diagnostic angles under the original problem constraints. However, aggressive diversification carries real engineering risks: unconstrained sampling often introduces malformed code, nonsensical approaches, or outright violations of baseline invariants. The test for any diversification strategy is whether it improves task success under a fixed compute and latency budget.

To conserve verification bandwidth, the runtime should prune redundant candidates early using structural and behavioral deduplication. Abstract syntax tree (AST) normalization strips away superficial differences such as variable names and whitespace. Behavioral clustering then evaluates candidates against common test inputs to detect identical runtime behavior. This filtering allowed a competitive code-generation system to condense tens of thousands of raw model outputs into a handful of viable submissions [@li2022alphacode]. Both techniques establish bounded equivalence relations, whether syntactic equivalence under canonicalization or behavioral agreement over a test suite. Such deduplication is sound whenever that relation preserves the specific property being evaluated.

### Selection policies {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-policies}

A runtime evaluates candidates using three primary mechanisms: direct execution checks, answer agreement (consensus voting), and learned ranking. System designers often combine these approaches, tailoring the pipeline to the available evidence and the cost of evaluation rather than treating them as fixed, sequential stages.

Direct checks evaluate a candidate deterministically against explicit specifications. A parser rejects malformed syntax; a type checker enforces interface contracts and memory invariants; an automated test harness measures dynamic behavior on specified inputs. Each check operates within a strictly defined domain: successful compilation proves structural validity but says nothing about whether a race condition was resolved, while a regression test validates only the execution paths covered by its test fixtures. Furthermore, candidate execution remains a governed action that requires sandbox isolation, strict timeouts, and privilege boundaries appropriate to the environment.

Answer agreement aggregates independent reasoning paths through consensus. In **self-consistency**\index{Self-consistency!definition}, the runtime samples multiple reasoning trajectories and selects the plurality answer [@wang2022self]. For arithmetic, symbolic logic, or standardized factual queries, the system normalizes the answer representation and takes the majority vote. However, consensus is merely a property of the sampled distribution: when a model harbors a systematic bias or flawed reasoning shortcut, multiple independent paths frequently converge on the exact same error. In software repairs, textual voting is a poor comparison rule; agreement on observed behaviors carries the test coverage limits just described, and a correct minority candidate deserves an execution check rather than being outvoted by plausible failures.

When deterministic checks cannot fully validate candidate quality, learned rankers and model-based judges provide heuristic evaluation. A learned reward model or a secondary large language model (LLM) judge (a model prompted to grade another model's output) can evaluate explanatory adequacy, score style, or prioritize promising patches before invoking costly regression suites. Nevertheless, a learned ranking remains a statistical estimate whose relevance must be evaluated on the target task distribution. A fundamental distinction exists between ranking candidates and accepting a solution. Ranking merely orders candidates from best to worst according to a scoring function; acceptance determines whether a candidate satisfies the operational requirements of the task. If an entire candidate pool is defective, selecting the highest-ranked member simply returns the best failure. Validating acceptance requires an objective verifier that yields an authoritative pass or fail verdict.

::: {#dfn-vol3-verifier-guided-selection .callout-definition title="Verifier-guided selection"}

***Verifier-guided selection***\index{Verifier-guided selection!definition}\index{Verifier!definition} is a selection policy that returns a candidate only when a **verifier**, a check whose criteria and observations the candidate cannot modify, passes it, and abstains when no candidate passes.

1.  **Significance**: Its success rate is capped by pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$, the chance the pool holds a passing candidate (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k), while the share of its selections that are correct depends on both the verifier's passing-set precision and the selection policy (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision). The fixed IID first-passing policy developed there preserves passing-set precision; ranking among passing candidates need not. Selection coverage and selected correctness together determine the probability of returning a valid result.
2.  **Distinction**: Voting selects what the generator produces most often and learned ranking selects what a scorer prefers; only a verifier's verdict can justify returning a candidate instead of abstaining.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the verifier's pass as task acceptance; the verdict covers the checked property, and its false acceptance rate grows in importance as the pool's valid-candidate rate falls.

:::

The hypothetical repair pool in @tbl-vol3-candidate-diversity illustrates how these distinct verification stages expose candidate quality. The checks are deliberately bounded: a focused reproducer exercises the known race condition, while broader regression suites remain untested.

| **Candidate** | **Proposed repair**                                | **Observed check result**       | **Supported conclusion**                                  |
|:--------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| A             | Increase the timeout                               | Compiles; known failure remains | Structural validity is insufficient                       |
| B             | Retry after the timeout                            | Compiles; known failure remains | Different code can preserve the same defect               |
| C             | Change notification handling with malformed syntax | Parsing fails                   | This artifact cannot proceed to execution testing         |
| D             | Change notification handling with valid syntax     | Compiles; reproducer passes     | Promising repair, with untested behavior still unresolved |

: **Evidence for candidate selection**: A hypothetical repair pool separates the proposed mechanism, the observed result, and the conclusion each check supports. {#tbl-vol3-candidate-diversity tbl-colwidths="[12,25,30,33]"}

A production runtime pipelines these checks to maximize rejection efficiency, ordering them by cost and filtering power rather than arbitrary conceptual categories. A lightweight structural check that parses syntax or validates an AST costs fractions of a millisecond and quickly discards malformed candidates, saving expensive sandboxed execution environments and high-latency LLM scoring passes from wasted work. However, pipeline ordering must reflect empirical systems profiling rather than intuition. For illustration, executing a compiled binary in a warm container might take 5 ms, whereas invoking a large model-based judge to evaluate code style is a full model call that might take 800 ms and consume a share of the token budget. Moreover, joint candidate comparison scales differently with context window size than scoring each candidate independently. Because verification overhead directly cuts into the runtime's available time and compute, candidate selection must be budgeted as an integral component of test-time compute.

### Candidate availability under pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k}

**pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$**\index{Pass at k!definition} measures the probability that at least one of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ sampled candidates passes the specified tests [@chen2021evaluating].[^fn-passk-metric-origin]

[^fn-passk-metric-origin]: **Origin of pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$**: The metric was introduced to score program synthesis by functional correctness rather than by textual similarity to a reference [@kulal2019spoc]. Because plugging the observed pass fraction $\PassingSampleCount/\GeneratedSampleCount$ into $1-(1-\PassingSampleCount/\GeneratedSampleCount)^\IndependentAttemptCount$ biases the estimate of what breadth buys, @chen2021evaluating replaced it with the combinatorial estimator derived below. \index{Pass at k!origin} It measures availability in the pool, not the success rate of the output a deployed selector returns.

For a fixed task and fixed generation policy, suppose independent samples each pass the tests with probability $\AttemptPassProbability$. The probability that all $\IndependentAttemptCount$ samples fail is $(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$, so

$$
\operatorname{pass@}\IndependentAttemptCount = 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount.
$$

This expression is conditional on that task and sampling policy. To summarize a workload with different task-level pass probabilities, average the task-level quantities; substituting the workload's average $\AttemptPassProbability$ generally gives a different result. For an adaptive policy that revises its prompt after feedback, evaluate the policy's resulting pools rather than assuming they follow this fixed-distribution formula.

In a benchmark, generate $\GeneratedSampleCount \ge \IndependentAttemptCount$ candidates for a task and let $\PassingSampleCount$ pass the fixed test criterion. Of the $\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}$ subsets of size $\IndependentAttemptCount$, exactly $\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}$ contain only failures. The subset estimator is therefore

$$
\PassAtKEstimate
= 1-\frac{\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}}{\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}},
$$

with the numerator taken as zero when $\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount<\IndependentAttemptCount$. Under independent, identically distributed sampling for the fixed task, this estimates the probability that a fresh pool of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ candidates contains a test-passing member without bias; @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pass-at-k derives this expectation and details evaluation without factorials. Benchmark results average these estimates over tasks [@chen2021evaluating].

The relationship to deployed selection follows from the event being measured. If the selector must return an unchanged member of the same pool, it cannot return a test-passing candidate when the pool contains none. Its probability of returning a test-passing candidate is therefore at most pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$, counting abstention as no returned pass. A selector that always finds a passing member whenever one exists reaches this ceiling; whether the deployed selector does, within the deployment's checking budget, is a separate measurement.

The predicate is passing these tests, which is narrower than satisfying the complete task requirements, and the ceiling covers only selectors that return an unchanged pool member; a selector that repairs candidates or synthesizes a new one generates additional artifacts. Report candidate availability alongside selected-output performance under the relevant criterion.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The distinction between pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ over a candidate pool and consistency over repeated system runs is developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-pass-k.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ttc_margin_pass_at_n.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Four horizontal green bars for pools of 1, 2, 4, and 8 candidates, labeled 30, 51, 76, and 94 percent."}

*Each doubling of the pool squares the chance that no candidate passes.*
:::

Breadth has a price that pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ makes easy to compute. In **best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling**\index{Best-of-N sampling!definition}, the runtime generates $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates for one decision and returns one that its selector admits. The pool is the same object pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ describes, so its availability is pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ with $\IndependentAttemptCount = \CandidatePoolSize$, written pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$ from here on. The notebook below prices that pool against the simplest alternative, generating one candidate at a time and stopping at the first pass, under the most favorable selection assumption: the verifier is the acceptance check itself.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-best-of-n-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PRICE OF A LARGER POOL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price; fallacies (mixed-workload pass@N).
# │ Goal: Compare parallel best-of-N with stop-at-first-pass sequential retry
# │       at the same success probability.
# │ Show: pass@N, marginal gain of the last candidate, candidates per success.
# │ How: IID candidates for a fixed task; the verifier is the acceptance check;
# │      a perfect selector returns a passing member whenever one exists.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class BestOfN:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    p = 0.30  # hypothetical per-candidate pass probability for a fixed task
    pools = (1, 2, 4, 8)  # pool sizes compared
    p_easy = 0.60  # hypothetical mixed workload: half the tasks pass at this rate
    p_hard = 0.0  # hypothetical mixed workload: the other half never pass

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_max = pools[-1]
    pass_at = []
    for n in pools:
        pass_at.append(1 - (1 - p) ** n)
    pass_max = pass_at[-1]
    last_gain = p * (1 - p) ** (n_max - 1)
    parallel_per_success = n_max / pass_max
    seq_candidates = pass_max / p  # expected attempts, stop at first pass, cap n_max
    seq_per_success = seq_candidates / pass_max  # reduces to 1 / p
    cost_ratio = parallel_per_success / seq_per_success
    p_mix = (p_easy + p_hard) / 2
    naive_mix = 1 - (1 - p_mix) ** n_max
    true_mix = ((1 - (1 - p_easy) ** n_max) + (1 - (1 - p_hard) ** n_max)) / 2

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pass_at == sorted(set(pass_at)), "pass@N rises with N")
    check(abs(seq_per_success - 1 / p) < 1e-12, "Sequential retry costs 1/p per success")
    check(cost_ratio > 2, "Parallel pool costs over twice as much per success")
    check(abs(p_mix - p) < 1e-12, "Mixed workload has the same average rate")
    check(true_mix < naive_mix - 0.3, "Averaging p overstates mixed-workload pass@N")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, precision=0, style="prose")
    n_max_str = fmt_int(n_max)
    pools_str = MarkdownStr(", ".join(str(n) for n in pools[:-1]) + ", and " + str(pools[-1]))
    pass_1_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[0]))
    pass_2_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[1]))
    pass_4_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[2]))
    pass_max_str = fmt_percent(pass_max, precision=1, style="prose")
    last_gain_pts_str = fmt(last_gain * 100, precision=1)
    parallel_per_success_str = fmt(parallel_per_success, precision=1)
    seq_candidates_str = fmt(seq_candidates, precision=2)
    seq_per_success_str = fmt(seq_per_success, precision=1)
    cost_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cost_ratio, precision=1)
    p_easy_str = fmt_percent(p_easy, precision=0, style="prose")
    naive_mix_str = fmt_percent(naive_mix, precision=1, style="prose")
    true_mix_str = fmt_percent(true_mix, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price .callout-notebook title="The price of a larger pool"}

**Problem**: Each candidate repair passes the task's verifier with probability $\AttemptPassProbability$, independently for this task, and the verifier is the acceptance check. How many candidates per accepted repair does a parallel pool of $\CandidatePoolSize$ spend, compared with sequential retry that stops at the first pass and gives up after $\CandidatePoolSize$ attempts?

**Variables**: $\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} BestOfN.p_str` (hypothetical); pools of `{python} BestOfN.pools_str` candidates; a selector that returns a passing member whenever one exists.

**Math**: The formula pass@$\CandidatePoolSize = 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\CandidatePoolSize$ gives `{python} BestOfN.pass_1_str`, `{python} BestOfN.pass_2_str`, `{python} BestOfN.pass_4_str`, and `{python} BestOfN.pass_max_str` for those pools. The last of `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates adds $\AttemptPassProbability(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^{\CandidatePoolSize-1}$, only `{python} BestOfN.last_gain_pts_str` percentage points. The parallel pool always spends `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates, or `{python} BestOfN.parallel_per_success_str` per accepted repair. Sequential retry fails only when all `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` attempts fail, so it reaches the same `{python} BestOfN.pass_max_str`, yet it spends on average $[1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\CandidatePoolSize]/\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} BestOfN.seq_candidates_str` candidates, or $1/\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} BestOfN.seq_per_success_str` per accepted repair.

**Systems insight**: At equal success, the parallel pool costs `{python} BestOfN.cost_mult_str` as much per accepted repair; what it buys is one round instead of an expected `{python} BestOfN.seq_candidates_str` sequential generate-and-check rounds. Breadth buys latency, not cost. In $\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$ it raises $\AcceptanceProbability$ per round but raises the attempt cost faster. Size $\CandidatePoolSize$ as the smallest pool whose pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$ meets the target within the rounds the deadline allows, and stop growing it once the next candidate's gain is worth less than its cost.

:::

### Selection and evidence costs {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-costs}

Expanding candidate breadth increases the likelihood that a valid solution enters the pool, but it simultaneously inflates the verification burden. Under a fixed deliberation budget, spending all resources on generation starves the verification stage, forcing the selector to rely on shallow heuristics. A smaller pool paired with informative, high-coverage checks frequently outperforms a large pool governed by weak selection. Conversely, when generation coverage is the primary bottleneck, expanding the pool yields immediate returns. Comparing these regimes requires evaluating the entire generation-and-selection policy rather than measuring either stage in isolation.

Checker errors compound rapidly as candidate pools grow. Every additional invalid candidate introduced into the pool provides another opportunity for an imperfect verifier to register a false pass. If a verifier has a 5 percent false acceptance rate (it passes 5 percent of invalid candidates, a rate defined formally in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision), evaluating twenty invalid proposals with independent check outcomes makes at least one false pass likely ($1 - (1 - 0.05)^{20} \approx 64\%$). Whether that false pass is actually returned depends on what else the pool holds and on the selection rule, a distinction that section makes exact. The ultimate error rate of the accepted solution depends on the base quality of the candidate distribution, the check's conditional error rates, and the rule used to break ties among passing candidates. When an adaptive search algorithm steers generation based on verifier feedback, it actively shifts all three factors, often optimizing directly against the verifier's blind spots.

Where the runtime gathers evidence dictates both the latency and the precision of selection. Validating only the final output may suffice when end-to-end execution checks are cheap and definitive. For extended multi-step trajectories, however, checking intermediate assumptions allows the runtime to prune failing branches before investing further compute. This establishes a fundamental design distinction between outcome checks that evaluate finished artifacts and process checks that govern multi-step execution.

## Candidate Verification {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification}

A search policy requires evidence that separates a genuinely correct candidate from a superficially plausible one. In a connection-pool repair, for instance, clean compilation confirms only syntactic and type validity; verifying that blocked worker threads actually wake up when a connection returns requires runtime execution. Even a targeted concurrency test explores only a subset of thread interleavings and can easily miss subtle race conditions. Every validation check answers a strictly bounded question. System designers must therefore decide which questions to ask, when to schedule each evaluation, and how the resulting evidence should redirect the remaining search budget.

### Outcome and step-level evidence {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-outcome-step-evidence}

An **outcome check**\index{Outcome check!definition} evaluates a completed candidate against an external criterion, such as whether a patched service passes an end-to-end regression test. In contrast, an **outcome reward model**\index{Outcome reward model!definition} predicts a scalar quality score for the completed candidate, functioning like the trained verifiers used to rank candidate solutions for mathematical reasoning [@cobbe2021training]. The check executes the candidate and reports what happened; the reward model only predicts how good the candidate is.

Step-level checks evaluate intermediate claims or state transitions. In our repair task, a check might verify whether a waiting worker receives a wake-up notification before the agent drafts a complex timeout adjustment. If an execution trace refutes the timeout hypothesis, the runtime can terminate that branch immediately, conserving generation tokens. Learned process scorers similarly rank or prune partial reasoning trajectories, treating low step scores as probabilistic signals of downstream failure. **Process supervision**\index{Process supervision!definition}[^fn-prm-step-labels] assigns feedback to discrete intermediate steps rather than deferring evaluation to terminal outcomes [@uesato2022solving; @lightman2023let]. The difference between outcome and process feedback lies in where the feedback attaches, not in what the evaluator may read, since a learned outcome scorer can also inspect the full reasoning trajectory before scoring the final output.

[^fn-prm-step-labels]: **Step-Level Labels (PRM800K)**: Outcome labels for code can be produced automatically by running tests. Step labels require a judgment on each intermediate step, and the PRM800K dataset used to train the process reward model of @lightman2023let contains about 800,000 human step-level labels. That labeling cost is one reason learned process scorers are scarcer than outcome checks. \index{Process reward model!labeling cost}

::: {#dfn-process-reward-model .callout-definition title="Process reward model (PRM)"}

A ***process reward model*** (PRM)\index{Process reward model!definition} is a learned scorer that assigns a value to each intermediate step of a candidate trajectory, conditioned on the task context and the preceding steps.

1.  **Significance**: Step scores allow search algorithms to prune unpromising branches early, keeping beam search and tree search, the search procedures that extend only the best-scoring partial candidates (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-search-structures), within finite computational budgets.
2.  **Distinction**: An outcome reward model evaluates only terminal states; a process reward model assigns credit across intermediate steps. This early steering capability requires dense step-level supervision, which costs substantially more to gather than automated test outcomes.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Mistaking a high step score for verified correctness. A process reward model provides heuristic guidance for ranking and pruning, but it offers no formal guarantees and satisfies no closure evidence level.

:::

Each verification granularity catches failures that the other overlooks. An outcome check evaluates global behavior, exposing subtle integration bugs that appear harmless when examined step by step. Conversely, a process check isolates errors early, preventing bad trajectories from consuming additional inference cycles. However, verifying too frequently consumes system resources and risks discarding viable candidate branches due to verifier noise. The system trade-off weighs avoided downstream generation against verification overhead and false rejections.

Computational cost also depends heavily on input scoping and prefix reuse. Consider a verifier that evaluates a task prompt of $\SequenceLength$ tokens and the candidate's growing prefix after each of its $\ScoredStepCount$ steps, with each step appending $\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$ tokens. Evaluating each cumulative prefix from scratch, without reusing key-value cache states from preceding steps, requires processing:

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{\ScoredStepCount}\left(\SequenceLength + \ScoredStepIndex\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength\right) = \ScoredStepCount \SequenceLength + \frac{\ScoredStepCount(\ScoredStepCount+1)}{2}\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength
$$ {#eq-vol3-prm-rescoring}

scorer input tokens, an overhead that scales quadratically with trajectory length $\ScoredStepCount$. The beam-search estimate later in this chapter (notebook \ref{nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs}) bills the $\ScoredStepIndex\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$ term of @eq-vol3-prm-rescoring, with the task prompt $\SequenceLength$ excluded, for every extension it scores at step $\ScoredStepIndex$. Incremental evaluation eliminates this quadratic burden when the serving engine supports prefix caching, reducing the marginal per-step cost to $\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$ tokens.
