Evaluators that require the complete candidate or lack cache-aware serving pay the full quadratic cost. Verification scheduling must therefore account directly for prompt length, caching efficiency, and invocation latency.

@Tbl-vol3-verifier-classes compares four common classes of checks by their inspection scope, failure modes, and deterministic guarantees, mapping each to the closure evidence levels defined in @sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure. Compilers and sealed test suites establish bounded, reproducible properties within their domains, whereas learned reward models serve strictly as heuristic ranking instruments.

| **Check**                | **Evaluates**                      | **Coverage**                              | **False-acceptance exposure**                    | **Deterministic**           | **Closure evidence level**                              |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Outcome scorer (learned) | Completed candidate                | Any representation it was trained to read | Persuasive but wrong final text                  | No                          | None; ranks only                                        |
| Process scorer (learned) | Intermediate step given its prefix | Steps it can delimit and judge            | Locally plausible steps that drift from the task | No                          | None; ranks and prunes only                             |
| Compiler or type checker | Syntax and declared types          | Properties expressible in the type system | Behavior outside the type system                 | Yes                         | Static analysis                                         |
| Sealed test suite        | Behavior on withheld cases         | The cases and schedules it exercises      | Untested inputs and schedules                    | Yes, under fixed conditions | Sealed tests, if the candidate cannot read or modify it |

: **Kinds of check and the claims they support**: Learned scorers order candidates; compilers and sealed suites establish bounded properties. None dominates the others on every task, and a deterministic verdict remains incomplete outside its coverage. {#tbl-vol3-verifier-classes tbl-colwidths="[17,17,18,20,11,17]"}

Selecting an effective check requires matching the observer's coverage directly to the failure modes that the application cannot tolerate.

### Check precision and the candidate pool {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision}

Structural validity does not guarantee task success. In search systems, the central reliability question is what fraction of the candidates that satisfy a given check truly solves the task. Define the event $\text{Valid}$ as meeting the task specification and $\text{PASS}$ as receiving a positive verifier verdict. Let $\ValidCandidateRate = \Pr(\text{Valid})$ denote the baseline rate of valid candidates within the candidate generator's distribution, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = \Pr(\text{PASS}\mid\neg\text{Valid})$ the **false acceptance rate**\index{False acceptance rate!definition}, and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = \Pr(\neg\text{PASS}\mid\text{Valid})$ the **false rejection rate**\index{False rejection rate!definition}. In this formulation, "acceptance" denotes an internal verifier outcome rather than an authorization to deploy code to production. The valid-candidate rate $\ValidCandidateRate$ is distinct from the test-pass probability $\AttemptPassProbability$ used in pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$. One concerns meeting the task specification; the other concerns passing the stated tests. An error-free check makes the two events coincide. Separating them is the point of this section.

The marginal probability of a positive verification result is $\VerifierPassProbability=\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$. Applying Bayes' rule yields the precision of positive verdicts:

$$
\VerifierPrecision \equiv \Pr(\text{Valid}\mid\text{PASS})
=\frac{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)}{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-verifier-precision}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ttc_margin_precision_base_rate.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A dark curve of the valid share among passing candidates plotted against the valid-candidate rate. It rises steeply at low rates and flattens near the top. The low-rate region is shaded red, and a red dot is labeled 5 percent valid, 70 percent of passes."}

*At a low valid rate, even a strict check passes many invalid candidates.*
:::

When the base rate of valid candidates is low, even a verifier with an apparently modest false acceptance rate produces a passing pool dominated by invalid proposals, the classic base-rate fallacy. The foundation-model chapter applied the same Bayes arithmetic to one checked patch, where a fallible checker barely moved the defect share (systems perspective \ref{psp-02-the-fallacy-of-correlated-self-verification}); @eq-vol3-verifier-precision is its complement, applied to every candidate in a pool. This is the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) in quantitative form. Producing a valid candidate and establishing that a passing candidate is valid are different events, and the base rate and the check's error rates, not the size of the pool, bound how far a pass can be trusted. Engineers must therefore measure error rates empirically for each target task, model family, and verification environment.

While @eq-vol3-verifier-precision governs the population of passing candidates, translating this metric into the expected reliability of the *selected* candidate requires specifying a selection policy. Consider independent and identically distributed candidate-check pairs for a given task, evaluated under fixed error rates. The runtime generates a batch, evaluates candidates in an arbitrary order independent of quality, and selects the first candidate that passes, abstaining if none succeeds. Under these assumptions, the precision conditional on making a selection equals $\VerifierPrecision$. Evaluating candidates in sequence reveals only that prior candidates failed; under independence, this search history does not alter the probability that the first passing candidate is valid. Conversely, selecting the candidate with the highest continuous reward score actively concentrates verifier measurement errors, a failure mode analyzed in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: compute-vol3-ttc-check-yield
# ┌── LEGO ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under
# │ Goal: Separate passing-set precision, selection coverage, and incident loss.
# │ Show: A hypothetical fixed-batch first-pass selection policy.
# │ How: IID candidate/check outcomes, fixed rates, abstention if none passes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check
import math

class CheckYield:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    n = 64
    tokens_per_candidate = 1_024 * token
    output_price = 15 * USD / Mtoken
    p = 0.05
    eps_fr = 0.10  # false rejection rate, epsilon_FR (hypothetical)
    eps_fa = 0.02  # false acceptance rate, epsilon_FA (hypothetical)
    incident_loss = 500 * USD

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Physics & Logic) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    valid_pass = p * (1 - eps_fr)
    invalid_pass = (1 - p) * eps_fa
    pass_probability = valid_pass + invalid_pass
    precision = valid_pass / pass_probability
    defect_given_selection = 1 - precision
    any_selection = 1 - (1 - pass_probability) ** n
    no_selection = 1 - any_selection
    wrong_selection = any_selection * defect_given_selection
    any_false_pass = 1 - (1 - invalid_pass) ** n
    expected_valid_passes = n * valid_pass
    expected_invalid_passes = n * invalid_pass
    expected_passes = n * pass_probability
    conditional_loss = defect_given_selection * incident_loss
    task_loss = wrong_selection * incident_loss
    output_bill = (n * tokens_per_candidate * output_price).to(USD)
    # Sensitivity: halve the false acceptance rate, or double the valid rate.
    precision_half_fa = valid_pass / (valid_pass + (1 - p) * eps_fa / 2)
    precision_double_p = 2 * p * (1 - eps_fr) / (2 * p * (1 - eps_fr) + (1 - 2 * p) * eps_fa)
    loss_to_bill = (task_loss / output_bill).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pass_probability > 0, "Passing-set precision requires q > 0.")
    check(isinstance(n, int) and n > 0, "n must be a positive int")
    check(all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (p, eps_fa, eps_fr)), "rates must be in [0, 1]")
    check(
        all(
            0 <= probability <= 1
            for probability in (
                valid_pass,
                invalid_pass,
                pass_probability,
                precision,
                defect_given_selection,
                any_selection,
                no_selection,
                wrong_selection,
                any_false_pass,
            )
        ),
        "probabilities must be in [0, 1]",
    )
    check(math.isclose(precision + defect_given_selection, 1), "precision + defect must sum to 1")
    check(math.isclose(any_selection + no_selection, 1), "any + no selection must sum to 1")
    check(0 <= expected_valid_passes <= n, "expected valid passes in bounds")
    check(0 <= expected_invalid_passes <= n, "expected invalid passes in bounds")
    check(0 <= expected_passes <= n, "expected passes in bounds")
    check(math.isclose(expected_valid_passes + expected_invalid_passes, expected_passes), "expected passes must sum")
    check(wrong_selection <= any_selection, "wrong selection <= any selection")
    check(wrong_selection <= any_false_pass, "wrong selection <= any false pass")
    check(math.isclose(wrong_selection, any_selection * defect_given_selection), "wrong selection identity")
    check(tokens_per_candidate > 0 * token, "tokens per candidate must be positive")
    check(output_price >= 0 * USD / Mtoken, "output price non-negative")
    check(output_bill >= 0 * USD, "output bill non-negative")
    check(0 * USD <= task_loss <= conditional_loss <= incident_loss, "loss hierarchy must hold")
    check(math.isclose(task_loss.to(USD).magnitude, (any_selection * conditional_loss).to(USD).magnitude), "task loss identity")
    check(precision < precision_half_fa < 1 and precision < precision_double_p < 1, "sensitivity ordering")
    check(loss_to_bill > 100, "loss to bill ratio > 100")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Human-Readable Outputs) ───────────────────────────────────
    n_str = fmt_int(n)
    tokens_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_candidate)
    price_str = fmt_usd(output_price * Mtoken)
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, style="prose")
    eps_fr_str = fmt_percent(eps_fr, style="prose")
    eps_fa_str = fmt_percent(eps_fa, style="prose")
    loss_str = fmt_usd(incident_loss)
    valid_passes_str = fmt(expected_valid_passes, precision=2)
    invalid_passes_str = fmt(expected_invalid_passes, precision=3)
    passes_str = fmt(expected_passes, precision=3)
    precision_str = fmt_percent(precision, precision=2, style="prose")
    defect_str = fmt_percent(defect_given_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    coverage_str = fmt_percent(any_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    abstention_str = fmt_percent(no_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    wrong_str = fmt_percent(wrong_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    any_false_str = fmt_percent(any_false_pass, precision=2, style="prose")
    conditional_loss_str = fmt_usd(conditional_loss, precision=2)
    task_loss_str = fmt_usd(task_loss, precision=2)
    bill_str = fmt_usd(output_bill, precision=2)
    precision_half_fa_str = fmt_percent(precision_half_fa, precision=1, style="prose")
    precision_double_p_str = fmt_percent(precision_double_p, precision=1, style="prose")
    loss_to_bill_str = fmt_int(round(loss_to_bill))
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under .callout-notebook title="Yield and risk under asymmetric verifier error"}

**Problem**: A repair policy generates all `{python} CheckYield.n_str` candidates before selection. It uses the first-passing rule above and abstains when no candidate passes. What does additional breadth buy, and what risk remains?

**Variables**: All rates are hypothetical. Each candidate contains `{python} CheckYield.tokens_str` tokens, billed at `{python} CheckYield.price_str` per million output tokens. The valid-candidate rate is `{python} CheckYield.p_str`, false rejection is `{python} CheckYield.eps_fr_str`, and false acceptance is `{python} CheckYield.eps_fa_str`. Suppose a separately authorized deployment policy deploys the selected candidate without further checking. A defective deployment incurs `{python} CheckYield.loss_str` in incident loss. For this calculation alone, valid deployments and abstentions incur zero incident loss, and missed repairs and delay are left unpriced.

**Math**: The expected passing counts are `{python} CheckYield.valid_passes_str` valid candidates and `{python} CheckYield.invalid_passes_str` invalid candidates, totaling `{python} CheckYield.passes_str`. @Eq-vol3-verifier-precision yields `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` precision. Conditional on making a selection, the probability of a defective selection is therefore `{python} CheckYield.defect_str`, with expected incident loss `{python} CheckYield.conditional_loss_str` per selected deployment.

The probability of any selection is $1-(1-\VerifierPassProbability)^\CandidatePoolSize$, or `{python} CheckYield.coverage_str`; the policy abstains on `{python} CheckYield.abstention_str` of batches. Multiplying selection coverage by conditional defect probability gives `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str` defective selections per task attempt and `{python} CheckYield.task_loss_str` expected incident loss per attempt, including abstentions. Generating the entire batch costs `{python} CheckYield.bill_str` in output charges. Input charges, checking, and other operational costs are omitted. A sequential policy that stops generation at the first pass would have a different generation bill.

**Systems insight**: Expected incident loss per attempt is about `{python} CheckYield.loss_to_bill_str` times the output bill, so the acceptance policy, not the token price, sets the cost of this task. Precision responds to two knobs of similar strength: halving the false acceptance rate raises it from `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` to `{python} CheckYield.precision_half_fa_str`, and doubling the valid-candidate rate raises it to `{python} CheckYield.precision_double_p_str`. More candidates move neither. At a low base rate, spend on whichever of a better generator or a stricter check is cheaper, and price false rejections too when a missed valid repair is costly.

:::

Holding $\ValidCandidateRate$, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$, and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate$ fixed, increasing the batch size $\CandidatePoolSize$ does not improve precision $\VerifierPrecision$. Expanding candidate breadth raises the probability of surfacing at least one passing candidate, but it simultaneously compounds the likelihood that the batch contains at least one false acceptance: $1-[1-(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate]^\CandidatePoolSize$. In our numerical scenario, that false-pass exposure reaches `{python} CheckYield.any_false_str`, whereas the actual probability of deploying a defective candidate is `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str`. Under a first-passing policy, a batch can contain invalid passes without consequence as long as an earlier valid candidate is evaluated and accepted first. System designers must distinguish candidate yield, verifier precision, and end-to-end deployment risk.

### Selection pressure on imperfect checks {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure}

The static distribution model serves as an engineering baseline, but adaptive search shifts the underlying distribution. A search policy that iteratively refines candidates to maximize an evaluation score alters the candidate population, driving proposals into regions where the evaluator is poorly calibrated. Under sustained selection pressure, the initial estimates of $\ValidCandidateRate$, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$, and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate$ no longer characterize the candidates that reach final evaluation. Optimization against imperfect proxy metrics degrades performance through distinct failure mechanisms [@manheim2018categorizing]. Manheim and Garrabrant formalize these phenomena as variants of Goodhart's law,[^fn-goodhart-law-origin] which observes that any metric optimized as a target loses its validity as a measurement. Three variants directly impact agentic systems: *regressional* Goodhart occurs when an argmax operator selects for positive measurement noise; *extremal* Goodhart emerges when correlations observed across typical candidates break down in the distributional tails explored by search; and *adversarial* Goodhart occurs when candidate code actively manipulates or bypasses the evaluation harness.

[^fn-goodhart-law-origin]: **Goodhart's Law**: The economist Charles Goodhart stated it in 1975 about monetary policy: any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes [@goodhart1984]. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later gave it the form usually quoted today, that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure [@strathern1997improving]. A test suite used to select patches is such a regularity, a reliable description of past candidates that weakens once search optimizes against it. \index{Goodhart's law!origin}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-argmax-selection
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTION ON A NOISY SCORE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure.
# │ Goal: Show how argmax selection concentrates positive scoring error, and
# │       how a rare checker gap becomes likely in a large pool.
# │ Show: Exact expected maximum of N standard normal errors; exploit presence.
# │ How: Numerical integration of N x phi(x) Phi(x)^(N-1); IID candidates.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
import math

def expected_max_std_normal(n, lo=-10.0, hi=10.0, steps=40_000):
    """Trapezoidal integral of x * n * phi(x) * Phi(x)**(n - 1)."""
    dx = (hi - lo) / steps
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(steps + 1):
        x = lo + i * dx
        pdf = math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
        cdf = 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2)))
        weight = 0.5 if i in (0, steps) else 1.0
        total += weight * x * n * pdf * cdf ** (n - 1)
    return total * dx

class ArgmaxSelection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_small = 4  # hypothetical small pool
    n_large = 64  # same batch size as the yield notebook
    gap_rate = 0.005  # hypothetical fraction of candidates exploiting a check gap

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    shift_small = expected_max_std_normal(n_small)
    shift_large = expected_max_std_normal(n_large)
    asym_large = math.sqrt(2 * math.log(n_large))
    gap_present = 1 - (1 - gap_rate) ** n_large

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(expected_max_std_normal(1)) < 1e-6, "Mean of one standard normal is zero")
    check(0 < shift_small < shift_large < asym_large, "Selected error grows with N, below the asymptote")
    check(0 < gap_present < 1, "Probability bounds")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    n_small_str = fmt_int(n_small)
    n_large_str = fmt_int(n_large)
    shift_small_str = fmt(shift_small, precision=1)
    shift_large_str = fmt(shift_large, precision=1)
    asym_large_str = fmt(asym_large, precision=1)
    gap_rate_str = fmt_percent(gap_rate, precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_present_str = fmt_percent(gap_present, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The regressional mechanism can be formulated analytically. Suppose a learned scorer reports an estimated utility $\EstimatedCandidateUtility_i = \CandidateUtility_i + \CandidateScoringError_i$ for candidate $\CandidateIndex$, where $\CandidateUtility_i$ represents genuine task utility and $\CandidateScoringError_i$ represents an independent scoring error with zero mean and standard deviation $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation$ (scoring noise, unrelated to the per-turn error rate of horizon compounding). Selecting $\arg\max_i \EstimatedCandidateUtility_i$ maximizes the combined sum, meaning the chosen candidate is disproportionately one that benefited from an unusually large positive error. For independent Gaussian errors, the expected maximum error among $\CandidatePoolSize$ proposals scales asymptotically as:

$$
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\max_{i \le \CandidatePoolSize} \CandidateScoringError_i\Bigr] \approx \ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}
$$ {#eq-vol3-argmax-noise}

for large $\CandidatePoolSize$.[^fn-gumbel-tail-growth] Expressed in units of $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation$, the exact numerical expectation is `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_small_str` for `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_small_str` candidates and reaches `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_large_str` for `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates, where the asymptotic expression predicts `{python} ArgmaxSelection.asym_large_str`. This expected maximum is an upper bound on the selected candidate's expected scoring error, attained when all candidates have equal true utility. When true utilities vary, selection depends on both utility and noise; Exercise 8 derives the selected error for one such distribution. An acceptance threshold calibrated on individual, unselected completions therefore requires re-evaluation on selected candidates, because argmax selection can concentrate positive verifier errors.

[^fn-gumbel-tail-growth]: **Extreme-Value Asymptotics**: The form $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$ is only the leading term of the Gaussian maximum, and convergence is slow, which is why the chapter computes the exact expectation beside it. The Gaussian is also a favorable case: scoring errors with heavier tails, such as a learned judge that occasionally misjudges badly, push the selected error up faster than $\sqrt{\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$, so the drift in a real pool can exceed this estimate. \index{Extreme value!argmax selection}

Rising selected scoring error does not by itself imply declining true utility. In Exercise 8(b), independent Gaussian utility and noise make both the winner's expected utility and its scoring error increase with pool size. Empirical evaluations of best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling against learned reward models show a different pattern: the optimized proxy score keeps increasing while an independent reference score initially improves, plateaus, and eventually degrades [@gao2023scaling]. That downturn depends on the joint distribution of utility and measurement error, or on checks that search can exploit; @eq-vol3-argmax-noise alone does not predict it. @Fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence sketches the empirical pattern, with a rising proxy score (dashed blue curve) and a held-out reference score (solid green curve) that peaks before declining.

::: {#fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection**: A qualitative sketch of the measured best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ pattern. The proxy score of the selected candidate keeps rising as $\CandidatePoolSize$ grows, while a held-out reference score rises and then declines. The widening gap illustrates proxy optimism under selection; the declining reference score is an empirical pattern, not a necessary consequence of growing scoring error. The axes carry no values, and the point where the reference score turns down depends on the task." fig-alt="Line sketch with candidates selected from, N, on a log-scale horizontal axis and score of the selected candidate on the vertical axis, without tick values. A dashed blue curve labeled proxy score rises and flattens. A solid green curve labeled held-out reference follows it at first, peaks near the middle at a marked dot, and then declines. The region between the curves is shaded, a red double-headed arrow at the right labels the gap scoring error of the winner, and a dashed line below the green peak notes that where the decline begins depends on the task."}
![](images/svg/goodhart_divergence.svg)
:::

Verifier blind spots compound across large candidate pools following the same binomial dynamics as the pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ metric. If an unmodeled edge case or exploit is present in a fraction $\ExploitCandidateFraction$ of proposals, a batch of $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates contains at least one exploiting solution with probability $1-(1-\ExploitCandidateFraction)^\CandidatePoolSize$. A vulnerability that appears in only `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_rate_str` of baseline candidates, practically invisible during single-shot testing, emerges in a batch of `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates with probability `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_present_str`. When an invalid candidate achieves a passing score by slipping through such a blind spot, competitive selection readily identifies and crowns it. Verifier accuracy measured on unselected baseline distributions systematically overstates verification reliability during search, and this divergence widens with candidate breadth.

In the connection-pool scenario, consider an agent attempting to fix a broken notification path. The test suite pass rate can increase because a patch fixes the missing wake-up signal, or because the patch deletes the unit test assertion that detects blocked worker threads. Both alterations improve the raw score, but only the first resolves the underlying defect. The candidate under evaluation must therefore remain strictly isolated from the verification criteria, preventing generated code from tampering with authoritative test definitions or synthesizing fabricated pass signals. When candidate code executes within the same process address space as the evaluation harness, it can monkey-patch runtime assertion routines, the most acute form of adversarial Goodhart. Verification cycles generate value only while the resulting evaluation evidence remains trustworthy and uncorrupted.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Grader isolation, which keeps test definitions, grading scripts, and pass signals outside the candidate's reach, is developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms-grader-isolation.
:::

Sandboxing the evaluator preserves verification integrity but does not expand its intrinsic coverage: a sealed regression suite still misses unexercised thread schedules, and a learned judge still risks favoring persuasive but erroneous code. Verification protocols must therefore measure the end-to-end outputs produced by the deployed search policy across target token budgets, accounting explicitly for false acceptances and abstentions. Increasing confidence requires orthogonal, independent verification mechanisms; evaluating another correlated heuristic score adds negligible informational value.

Effective verification also yields fine-grained execution artifacts that subsequent search stages can reuse, including specific contradicted hypotheses, verified sub-invariants, and passing regression subsets. When an agent refines a candidate, localized modifications often leave earlier sub-verifications intact. Explicitly modeling these verification dependencies allows the search runtime to selectively invalidate obsolete assertions while preserving valid intermediate proofs, avoiding the computational overhead of rescoring unchanged reasoning trajectories from scratch.

## Revisable Candidate Plans {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision}

Validation checks often challenge intermediate premises rather than merely rejecting a final answer. Suppose a software repair agent formulates a diagnosis, writes a patch, and outlines a test plan to resolve a connection-pool leak. When a targeted regression test contradicts the initial diagnosis, discarding the entire proposal wastes previous computation and discards valid discoveries. Conversely, retaining the unrevised plan leaves downstream logic anchored to a disproven assumption. To resolve this tension, the agent runtime must isolate the candidate artifacts that depend on the invalid premise before determining the scope of subsequent model invocations.

A **revisable candidate plan**\index{Revisable candidate plan!definition} makes these causal dependencies explicit. Rather than recording past execution history, it tracks unexecuted candidate operations alongside the specific evidence supporting each step. When new evidence undermines a premise, the runtime invalidates and regenerates only the affected subgraphs while preserving supported artifacts. The newly generated components must then satisfy the same verification checks as the original plan. This architecture descends directly from truth maintenance systems, which maintain explicit justifications for each inference so that retracting a premise automatically invalidates every conclusion resting upon it [@doyle1979truth].

### Candidate dependency graphs {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-plan-graph}

Consider an agent candidate that attributes a connection-pool exhaustion failure to an overly short client timeout. The runtime organizes the candidate's internal structure as a directed acyclic graph, placing directed edges from each prerequisite to the artifact that relies on it. @Tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies illustrates this organization. In this graph, the repository source excerpt, the initial failure log, and the test inventory are externally supplied inputs, whereas the diagnosis, the patch candidate, and the selected verification checks are generated artifacts. The graph formalizes causal relationships among these components without requiring the underlying model's autoregressive reasoning to mirror the same explicit structure.

| Artifact                | Direct prerequisites                        | What the artifact contributes                                     |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source excerpt          | Repository revision and file identity       | The implementation being considered                               |
| Diagnosis               | Source excerpt and failure observation      | A proposed explanation of the failure                             |
| Patch candidate         | Source excerpt and diagnosis                | A proposed change to that implementation                          |
| Test inventory          | Repository revision (a supplied input)      | The tests available for selection                                 |
| Check selection         | Patch candidate and test inventory          | Checks intended to distinguish this repair from an inadequate one |
| API compatibility notes | Task constraints and public API declaration | Restrictions that every acceptable repair must preserve           |
: **Dependencies within a repair candidate**: Each row names the inputs needed to interpret its artifact. A separate compatibility branch can be retained only while its own inputs remain applicable. {#tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies}

Now suppose a targeted concurrency test reveals that an idle connection became available while a waiting worker remained blocked past its notification threshold. This observation directly refutes the timeout hypothesis: the root cause is a missed wake-up notification rather than an aggressive timer. Because both the timeout patch and its associated check selection depend directly on the refuted diagnosis, the runtime marks them as invalid and schedules them for reconsideration. At the same time, the source excerpt remains valid because the underlying repository file has not changed, and the API compatibility analysis remains sound because public interface constraints have not shifted. The runtime constructs the next inference prompt by supplying the still-valid inputs alongside the new test observation, requesting an updated diagnosis, patch, and test suite. The new candidate artifacts are then subjected to independent verification.

Maintaining rigorous dependency tracking is essential. An incomplete graph with missing edges retains stale conclusions just as easily as an unmanaged prompt buffer. For example, if an apparently decoupled compatibility branch relies on method signatures modified by the new patch, omitting that dependency edge leaves invalidated compatibility claims in place. Explicit dependency management proves valuable precisely when the runtime overhead of maintaining the graph and traversing invalidation paths is smaller than the latency and token cost of recomputing unaffected candidate branches.

### Evidence preconditions {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-precondition-invalidation}

The runtime must distinguish an actively contradicted claim from an observation that has simply expired or become irrelevant. A failing unit test directly refutes the hypothesis that a proposed patch resolves the defect. In contrast, a previously successful test run on an earlier candidate remains a valid historical measurement of that specific candidate, but provides zero evidence for the current variant. Disentangling historical observations from active plan validation prevents cached test successes from erroneously endorsing unverified code changes.

To guarantee sound reuse, every observation recorded during a repair task must capture its complete provenance: the exact source revision or patch digest, test suite version, compiler flags, and runtime environment configuration. Similarly, an observation derived from reading a file must bind to the cryptographic hash of the file contents at the moment of inspection, rather than to a mutable filesystem path that could be modified concurrently.

When an input artifact changes or an assumption fails, the runtime marks that node as unsupported and traverses the dependency edges to identify all downstream artifacts requiring re-evaluation. If an artifact node $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ loses its supporting evidence, the set of invalidated artifacts is precisely its reachable descendants in the graph: $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode) = \{\ReachableArtifactNode \mid \InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode\}$, where $\InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode$ indicates that a directed path leads from $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ to $\ReachableArtifactNode$. A breadth-first search computes $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ in time linear in the number of vertices and edges.[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies] All nodes outside $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ retain their validity, preserving independent subgraphs such as the API compatibility analysis. A candidate graph of dozens or hundreds of nodes, like the schema in @tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies, is traversed in a tiny fraction of the illustrative `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` it takes to generate a single token. The engineering burden therefore lies not in graph search but in capturing dependency edges accurately. In the repair, the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis, traversal marks its only descendants, the patch and its check selection, for review, and the next request regenerates the diagnosis and that branch from the retained inputs (@fig-vol3-plan-revision).

[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies]: **Dependency-Driven Rebuilding**: Build tools solved the same problem for files. Make rebuilds a target only when one of its declared prerequisites is newer than the target [@feldman1979make], and its characteristic failure is the one described here: an undeclared dependency leaves a stale target that looks up to date. The saving is only as sound as the recorded edges. \index{Make!dependency tracking}

::: {#fig-vol3-plan-revision fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration**: In (A), the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis. Following the recorded dependency edges marks the patch and check selection for review, while the recorded inputs and the separately derived API notes keep their support. In (B), a new request supplies that supported frontier and regenerates only the diagnosis, patch, and check selection. The graph records candidate artifacts, not executed operations, and each replacement must still pass its own checks. The test inventory that also feeds check selection is omitted." fig-alt="Two stacked panels with the same dependency graph. Inputs on the left are source excerpt, failure observation, waiter-return test, and API declaration. In panel A, source excerpt and failure observation feed a red diagnosis marked timeout too short, which feeds a patch candidate and then a check selection; source excerpt also feeds the patch candidate. The patch candidate and check selection are drawn with dashed red borders, labeled needs review, inside a dashed region labeled Desc of diagnosis. The waiter-return test points to the diagnosis with a dashed red arrow labeled contradicts. The API declaration feeds API notes labeled support kept. In panel B, a dashed blue region labeled regenerated contains diagnosis prime labeled missed notification, patch candidate prime labeled notify on return, and check selection prime labeled ordering test; the same inputs, now including the waiter-return test, feed diagnosis prime, and API notes are labeled retained."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-plan-revision.svg)
:::

Explicit version identifiers and environment hashes make artifact invalidation deterministic, but an observation is only as reliable as its boundary assumptions. For instance, an integration test that queries an external network service may fail to reproduce even if local repository files remain bit-identical. Conversely, an edit to an unrelated documentation file should not invalidate unit test results whose code paths and inputs were unaffected. Safe artifact reuse depends on verifying the full operational context (sandbox isolation, mock definitions, and declared inputs) rather than relying solely on timestamps or file paths.

Systems architects must also maintain a strict distinction between planning representations and physical execution state. The candidate graph tracks uncommitted hypotheses and their supporting rationales; in contrast, reading source files, modifying a filesystem, or running integration binaries in a sandbox produce concrete external side effects. Removing an invalidated candidate node from memory does not undo a filesystem modification or release an allocated cloud container. The agent runtime must manage physical idempotency, rollback, and cleanup through dedicated failure recovery protocols.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Compensation and cleanup of external effects that outlive an abandoned candidate branch are developed in @sec-vol3-failure-recovery-branch-compensation.
:::

### Revision scope {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics}

When initiating a scoped revision, the runtime constructs a targeted prompt containing the current task constraints, the still-valid upstream frontier, the empirical observations that invalidated prior hypotheses, and the precise set of nodes marked for replacement. In the connection-pool scenario, the model is prompted for an alternative failure diagnosis, a corresponding patch, and an updated verification suite, omitting unchanged API definitions and repository metadata. Once the model returns candidates, the runtime verifies both that the replacements align with the retained artifacts and that their newly declared prerequisites are satisfied. A replacement that appears locally valid may still introduce latent incompatibilities with preserved downstream nodes.

Revision mechanisms operate across three distinct tiers based on the extent of invalidation:

1. A **local repair**\index{Local repair!definition} modifies a single node while preserving its outward interface and behavioral contracts, ensuring its dependents remain valid. A typical example is replacing a malformed shell command with an equivalent invocation that produces the expected exit code, leaving the overall dependency topology unaltered.
2. A **subgraph resynthesis**\index{Subgraph resynthesis!definition} invalidates a target node and all its descendants. The runtime supplies the model with the intact boundary frontier and requests a generative bridge from those validated inputs to the desired terminal objectives. In our connection-pool example, this tier discards the diagnosis, patch, and test plan while preserving the source context and API compatibility constraints.
3. **Stopping deliberation**\index{Stopping deliberation!definition} applies when new evidence undermines a foundational premise of the entire task, such as a required system dependency missing from the host environment or container credentials that lack necessary write permissions. No topological revision of the plan can recover validity, so the runtime ends deliberation and escalates the failure or reports the task as unresolvable under its operating contract rather than spending further inference tokens.

The decision flowchart in @fig-vol3-hierarchical-revision triages these three responses by screening candidate artifacts against two concrete operational checks: whether downstream dependents still have their preconditions met, and whether the task's underlying premises remain intact.

::: {#fig-vol3-hierarchical-revision fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Choosing the Revision Scope**: Two questions about the new evidence select among three responses. If the artifact's dependents still have what they need, a local repair replaces it alone. If they do not but the task's premises hold, subgraph resynthesis replaces the artifact and its descendants. If a premise has failed, deliberation stops and the task is reported unresolved or escalated. The tiers classify responses by how much support the evidence removes rather than establishing an unconditional preference for minimal edits." fig-alt="Flowchart. An amber box reading new evidence removes support from an artifact leads to a diamond asking whether dependents' needs are still met. Yes leads down to a card labeled local repair. No leads right to a second diamond asking whether task premises still hold. Yes leads down to a card labeled subgraph resynthesis. No leads by a red arrow to a red card labeled stop deliberation. Each card draws the same small dependency graph, a premise square feeding a chain of three artifact nodes and one side node. In local repair only the first chain node is filled and outlined as replaced, with the caption replace one artifact. In subgraph resynthesis the whole chain is filled and outlined, with the caption replace artifact plus descendants. In stop deliberation the premise square is red and every node is dashed, with the caption report unresolved or escalate. An arrow along the bottom runs from less support removed to more support removed."}
![](images/svg/hierarchical_revision_mechanics.svg)
:::

While local repair minimizes token generation, it is not universally the optimal strategy. If an invalidation strikes at the foundational framing of a problem, or if the candidate dependency graph has grown complex and unreliable, performing full regeneration from scratch often yields a more coherent artifact that is easier to validate. However, full regeneration forces the model to reproduce already-settled material, risking accidental regressions in code sections that were previously correct. Deciding between localized revision and complete regeneration requires weighing the scope of invalidated dependencies against the combined latency, token budget, and validation cost of resynthesizing the candidate.

```{python}
#| label: lego-candidate-plan-revision
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CANDIDATE PLAN REVISION OUTPUT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics,
# │          nbk-03-compute-and-token-savings-of.
# │ Goal: Compare output tokens for full and scoped candidate regeneration.
# │ Show: Generated token counts, retained output share, and avoided output.
# │ How: Hypothetical equal-sized nodes; only replaced nodes are generated.
# │ Note: Excludes input processing, checks, scheduling, and physical effects.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class PlanRevision:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    total_nodes = 12  # hypothetical complete candidate size
    replacement_nodes = 3  # hypothetical affected subset
    tokens_per_node = 150 * count  # hypothetical generated tokens per node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    full_output = total_nodes * tokens_per_node
    local_output = replacement_nodes * tokens_per_node
    output_share = (local_output / full_output).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    avoided_share = 1 - output_share

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < replacement_nodes <= total_nodes, "replacement nodes within total")
    check(local_output <= full_output, "local output <= full output")
    check(0 <= avoided_share < 1, "avoided share in [0, 1)")

    # ┌── 4. EXPORT (Narrative Values) ─────────────────────────────────────
    total_nodes_str = fmt_count(total_nodes)
    replacement_nodes_str = fmt_count(replacement_nodes)
    tokens_per_node_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_node)
    full_output_str = fmt_tokens(full_output)
    local_output_str = fmt_tokens(local_output)
    output_share_str = fmt_percent(output_share, style="prose")
    avoided_share_str = fmt_percent(avoided_share, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-and-token-savings-of .callout-notebook title="Output cost of a local plan revision"}

**Problem**: Suppose a candidate contains `{python} PlanRevision.total_nodes_str` nodes, each requiring `{python} PlanRevision.tokens_per_node_str` generated tokens. New evidence leaves `{python} PlanRevision.replacement_nodes_str` nodes needing replacement. How much output does scoped regeneration avoid if either approach produces a candidate adequate for the same subsequent checks?

**Math**: Multiplying the complete node count by the output per node gives `{python} PlanRevision.full_output_str` tokens for full regeneration. Multiplying the replacement count by the same output allowance gives `{python} PlanRevision.local_output_str` tokens for scoped regeneration. The scoped request generates `{python} PlanRevision.output_share_str` of the full request's output, avoiding `{python} PlanRevision.avoided_share_str` of that output under the equal-node-size assumption.

**Systems insight**: Scoped regeneration saves exactly the fraction of the plan that keeps its support. The saving shrinks linearly as the contradicted premise reaches more descendants and vanishes when every node depends on it, so once most of the plan shares the rejected assumption, full regeneration costs little more and is easier to check. The count covers generated plan tokens only; input to interpret retained constraints, integration, and checking are charged to both options.

:::

This idealized model isolates the immediate generation savings of localized regeneration. In production systems, however, those savings must be weighed against the overhead of tracking dynamic dependencies, assembling specialized prompts with retained context, and executing verification tests on hybrid plans. When a candidate plan transitions from deliberative search to actual execution, it stops being an uncommitted dependency graph and becomes active runtime state, which the agent harness manages and durable execution persists across infrastructure faults.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Persisting committed plan state across worker and infrastructure faults is developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution.
:::

### Limits on repeated revision {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-replanning-thrashing}

Iterative plan revision risks degenerating into unproductive replanning cycles. Without explicit termination policies, a model can oscillate between conflicting diagnoses, generate cosmetically distinct patches that suffer from identical logical flaws, or churn compute by reacting to non-fatal compiler warnings. The runtime must determine whether a newly proposed revision reflects genuine evidence updates or merely stochastic variation. A diagnostic warning warrants plan revision only when it directly challenges a core premise of the candidate; its severity tag alone should not trigger regeneration.

To prevent thrashing, the runtime enforces strict budget ceilings across model invocations, cumulative token counts, execution checks, and elapsed wall-clock time. Every attempted revision, including a failed local repair, consumes a portion of this allowance, and the same ceilings later bound the search as a whole (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-early-exit). Once the budget is exhausted, the deliberative loop terminates, either reporting the task as unresolvable or triggering an authorized human-in-the-loop escalation while leaving the unverified candidate unmerged. Furthermore, detecting identical or isomorphic proposals under unchanged environmental observations serves as an immediate trigger to halt search, whereas revisiting a previously explored proposal after new test evidence has emerged constitutes a valid re-evaluation.

Explicit dependency graphs let the runtime retain proven artifacts and spend compute only where a hypothesis failed. Revision, however, improves one candidate at a time. When several partial candidates compete for the same budget, the runtime must also decide which to extend and which to abandon, account for work it has already admitted, and know when to stop extending any of them.

## Bounded Search {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search}

The repair agent now holds several partial candidates at once, some freshly revised and some untouched. At each decision point it can generate an entirely new patch, extend an existing partial candidate by one step, or execute a diagnostic probe to disambiguate competing failure explanations. Each option draws against the same finite task budget while imposing distinct scheduling constraints and dependencies. A diagnostic check that gates the next code extension sits squarely on the critical path. In contrast, candidate generation requests can execute concurrently across available worker pools, whereas abandoning an unviable branch still incurs the unrecoverable cost of the tokens and runtime work already spent. Designing an effective search policy therefore requires explicit mechanisms to track admitted work, quantify pending resource consumption, and enforce principled stopping criteria.

### Search structures {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-search-structures}

Flat sampling generates a fixed pool of complete candidates before running selection logic across them. In best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$, the runtime admits at most $\CandidatePoolSize$ independent generation requests and applies a selector once all candidates finish. Because the requests share no execution dependencies, available serving capacity translates directly into reduced turnaround time through concurrent batching, provided the serving cluster can absorb the concurrent load without degrading token throughput. However, flat sampling defers all semantic evaluation until generation finishes. A candidate with a fatal flaw in its first five tokens still runs to completion, expending accelerator memory bandwidth and decode cycles that early validation could have saved.

**Beam search**\index{Beam search!definition}[^fn-beam-search-harpy] exposes that intermediate decision boundary directly. The runtime maintains a frontier of partial candidates bounded by a fixed beam width $\BeamWidth$. At each step, it generates a bounded set of extensions for each active candidate, evaluates the extended prefixes using a scoring function, and retains only the top-$\BeamWidth$ candidates for the next round. If fewer candidates survive pruning than the beam capacity allows, the runtime advances only the viable survivors; the search root itself typically begins below full beam width. Step scores can combine learned model probabilities with deterministic checks available at that execution boundary. The beam width bounds the active frontier that receives subsequent generation work rather than total ephemeral state: during expansion, the system must temporarily hold $\BeamWidth$ times the branching factor in candidate extensions, along with their KV cache state, scores, and parent references.

Early pruning trades generation compute for evaluation overhead and introduces a strict dependence on intermediate scoring accuracy. If a scoring pass mistakenly discards a prefix that would have yielded an optimal solution, a bounded beam search cannot recover that path unless the search policy explicitly incorporates backtracking. Conversely, terminating an unviable patch early avoids the cost of full candidate synthesis and subsequent integration tests. Early pruning yields net savings whenever intermediate evaluations cost less than the downstream generation they preempt, while maintaining an acceptably low false-rejection rate on viable prefixes.

[^fn-beam-search-harpy]: **Beam Search**: The method first appeared in the HARPY speech recognition system, which advanced only a small set of the best-scoring partial paths at each step instead of the full search space [@lowerre1976]. It accepted a bounded risk of pruning the eventual best path in exchange for bounded time and memory, the same trade a runtime makes when it retains a fixed number of partial candidates. \index{Beam search!origin}

An adaptive tree policy removes the constraint of expanding every retained candidate uniformly. Tree search over intermediate reasoning steps [@yao2023tree] dynamically steers computational effort toward branches with promising score trajectories, high outcome uncertainty, or diagnostic value for unresolved choices. **Monte Carlo tree search**\index{Monte Carlo tree search!definition} [@coulom2006efficient; @kocsis2006bandit] provides a formal framework for tracking visit counts and backpropagating estimated returns across a search graph. A prominent selection policy, the PUCT variant[^fn-puct-prior-bonus] used in AlphaGo [@silver2016mastering], traverses the tree from the root by selecting at each partial state $\PolicyObservedState$ the action $\PolicyAction$ that maximizes

$$
\TreeSearchMeanReturn(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction) + \TreeSearchExplorationWeight\,\TreeSearchPriorDistribution(\PolicyAction \mid \PolicyObservedState)\,\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{\SiblingPolicyAction} \TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\SiblingPolicyAction)}}{1 + \TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)},
$$ {#eq-vol3-puct}

where $\TreeSearchMeanReturn(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)$ represents the empirical mean return observed through extension $\PolicyAction$, $\TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)$ is its visit count, $\TreeSearchPriorDistribution(\PolicyAction \mid \PolicyObservedState)$ denotes a prior distribution over extensions (such as the base model's proposal probability for that reasoning step), and $\TreeSearchExplorationWeight$ is a positive scaling factor balancing exploitation of high-value paths against exploration of plausible but under-sampled branches. The vocabulary comes from reinforcement learning. The **leaf value** $\TreeSearchLeafScore$\index{Leaf value!definition} is a score of a partial candidate, supplied by a process scorer or by a check run at that point, and the "return" that $\TreeSearchMeanReturn$ averages is the leaf value reported by each visit through the edge. When the runtime evaluates a newly reached leaf node and obtains value $\TreeSearchLeafScore$, every edge along the trajectory back to the root updates its visit count ($\TreeSearchVisitCount \leftarrow \TreeSearchVisitCount + 1$) and its running mean value ($\TreeSearchMeanReturn \leftarrow \TreeSearchMeanReturn + (\TreeSearchLeafScore - \TreeSearchMeanReturn)/\TreeSearchVisitCount$). If $\TreeSearchLeafScore$ originates from an imperfect learned scorer, the $\TreeSearchMeanReturn$ term in @eq-vol3-puct inherits the selection drift formalized in @eq-vol3-argmax-noise, biasing visits toward edges whose scores are elevated by estimation noise. While tree search focuses compute where value signals appear strongest, its utility hinges on whether the resulting allocation improvements outweigh the latency and memory overhead of leaf evaluations and graph state management.

[^fn-puct-prior-bonus]: **From UCT to PUCT**: The UCT rule treated each node's choice of extension as a multi-armed bandit, adding an exploration bonus that shrinks as an extension accumulates visits [@kocsis2006bandit]. PUCT weights that bonus by a predictor's prior over the arms [@rosin2011multi], which is what lets a language model's own step probabilities concentrate a small budget on plausible extensions. A miscalibrated prior steers visits away from correct but unlikely steps just as effectively. \index{Monte Carlo tree search!PUCT}

The three structures differ chiefly in where pruning happens (@fig-vol3-search-topologies). Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ defers selection until every candidate is complete, beam search prunes partial candidates at each step boundary, and tree search expands one favored leaf at a time and updates visit counts along its path. Those pruning points in turn set each structure's concurrency, retained state, and prefix sharing (@tbl-vol3-search-topologies).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Radix prefix caching, which lets later requests for a branch reuse the KV state of its shared ancestors, is developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-radix-lookup.
:::

::: {#fig-vol3-search-topologies fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where Each Search Structure Prunes**: Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ generates complete candidates independently and discards all but the selected one only at the end. Beam search generates the beam width times the extensions per candidate at each step, scores them, and keeps the beam width. Tree search expands the leaf its selection rule favors, evaluates it, and updates visit counts and value estimates along the path to the root. The drawings show structure only; the pool size, beam width, and depth are illustrative." fig-alt="Three panels of node diagrams. Best-of-N: a prompt node branches into four chains of three generated nodes each; past a dashed line labeled select, one final node is marked selected and three are marked pruned. Beam: a prompt node branches into two nodes, each of which generates two children; a dashed line labeled score, keep 2 marks two children pruned, the two survivors each generate two more, and a second dashed line labeled keep 2 marks two retained and two pruned. Tree search: an uneven tree in which one path from the prompt is drawn bold and ends at a new leaf labeled evaluated V, with a note that the bold path updates N sub visit, the visit count, and Q; other nodes are drawn dashed as not yet expanded. A legend identifies prompt, generated, retained or selected, generated then pruned, and not yet expanded nodes."}
![](images/svg/search_topologies_comparison.svg)
:::

| **Structure**                | **Where pruning happens**                | **Concurrency**                               | **Search state**                                         | **Prefix sharing**                       |
|:-----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ | After complete candidates, at selection  | All $\CandidatePoolSize$ requests independent | $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates and their check results  | The common prompt only                   |
| Beam                         | At each step boundary, by step score     | Within a step; stages wait for scoring        | Up to width times extensions before pruning, plus scores | Each retained prefix with its extensions |
| Tree search                  | Adaptively, by value estimate and visits | Irregular; depends on which leaves are chosen | Tree nodes with visit counts and value estimates         | Every node's ancestors along its path    |

: **Search structures compared**: Each structure moves the pruning decision to a different point and holds different state. Concurrency describes the dependency graph; actual overlap depends on service capacity. {#tbl-vol3-search-topologies tbl-colwidths="[13,22,21,23,21]"}

### Pruned tree growth {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-pruned-tree
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRUNED TREE GROWTH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth.
# │ Goal: Show how a step check's rejection rate bounds expected tree size.
# │ Show: Unpruned leaf explosion; effective branching factor; generated nodes.
# │ How: Independent rejection of each child; generated nodes are b times the
# │      surviving parents at each depth; equal-sized steps.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class PrunedTree:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    wide_b = 4  # hypothetical alternatives per step, unpruned illustration
    wide_depth = 10  # hypothetical steps, unpruned illustration
    b = 5  # hypothetical children proposed per retained node
    p_prune = 0.68  # hypothetical probability a step check rejects a child
    depth = 3  # hypothetical steps in the worked example

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    wide_leaves = wide_b**wide_depth
    b_eff = b * (1 - p_prune)
    critical_prune = 1 - 1 / b
    unpruned_generated = 0
    pruned_generated = 0.0
    for d in range(1, depth + 1):
        unpruned_generated += b**d
        pruned_generated += b * b_eff ** (d - 1)
    unpruned_leaves = b**depth
    pruned_leaves = b_eff**depth
    generated_saving = 1 - pruned_generated / unpruned_generated

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(wide_leaves > 1_000_000, "Unpruned illustration exceeds a million leaves")
    check(b_eff > 1, "Worked example remains supercritical")
    check(p_prune < critical_prune, "Rejection rate is below the subcritical threshold")
    check(pruned_generated < unpruned_generated, "Pruning reduces generated nodes")
    check(generated_saving > p_prune, "Node saving exceeds the per-child rejection rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    wide_b_str = fmt_int(wide_b)
    wide_depth_str = fmt_int(wide_depth)
    wide_leaves_str = fmt_int(wide_leaves)
    b_str = fmt_int(b)
    p_prune_str = fmt_percent(p_prune, precision=0, style="prose")
    depth_str = fmt_int(depth)
    b_eff_str = fmt(b_eff, precision=1)
    critical_prune_str = fmt_percent(critical_prune, precision=0, style="prose")
    unpruned_generated_str = fmt_int(unpruned_generated)
    pruned_generated_str = fmt(pruned_generated, precision=1)
    unpruned_leaves_str = fmt_int(unpruned_leaves)
    pruned_leaves_str = fmt(pruned_leaves, precision=1)
    generated_saving_str = fmt_percent(generated_saving, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ttc_margin_pruned_nodes.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal orange bars. Unpruned: 155 generated nodes. Pruned: 25.8 generated nodes."}

*Each rejected child also removes the subtree it would have grown.*
:::

Pruning is what keeps a search tree from exploding. A search graph that unconditionally expands every node into `{python} PrunedTree.wide_b_str` branches across `{python} PrunedTree.wide_depth_str` successive steps yields `{python} PrunedTree.wide_leaves_str` leaves, quickly exhausting memory capacity and compute budgets. Now consider a system where each node proposes $\SearchBranchingFactor$ candidate extensions, and an intermediate validation check independently prunes each child with probability $\ChildPruningProbability$. The expected number of surviving branches per expanded node, the **effective branching factor**\index{Effective branching factor!definition}, becomes

$$
\EffectiveBranchingFactor = \SearchBranchingFactor\,(1 - \ChildPruningProbability).
$$ {#eq-vol3-effective-branching}

Under @eq-vol3-effective-branching, the expected frontier width at depth $\SearchDepthIndex$ is $\EffectiveBranchingFactor^{\,\SearchDepthIndex}$. Because each of the surviving nodes at depth $\SearchDepthIndex-1$ generates and validates $\SearchBranchingFactor$ proposed children, the total expected count of generated nodes through depth $\SearchDepth$ is $\sum_{\SearchDepthIndex=1}^{\SearchDepth} \SearchBranchingFactor\,\EffectiveBranchingFactor^{\,\SearchDepthIndex-1}$. This formulation defines a classic Galton–Watson branching process.[^fn-galton-watson-extinction] When $\EffectiveBranchingFactor < 1$, which requires a pruning rate above the critical threshold $1 - 1/\SearchBranchingFactor$, the frontier contracts geometrically with depth, causing the search tree to extinguish spontaneously. When $\EffectiveBranchingFactor > 1$, the frontier expands exponentially, requiring hard caps on depth, token consumption, or elapsed execution time to force termination.

[^fn-galton-watson-extinction]: **Galton–Watson Process**: The model comes from a Victorian question about the extinction of family surnames, analyzed in 1875 [@watson1875probability]. That analysis wrongly concluded that every line dies out; the correct result is the threshold used here, under which extinction is certain when the mean number of surviving offspring is at most one (excluding the degenerate case of exactly one child every time) and avoidable when it exceeds one. For a search tree the surviving offspring are the children that pass the step check, so the rejection rate decides which side of the threshold the search lands on. \index{Galton–Watson process!search trees}

To see this quantitative effect in practice, consider a concrete configuration where each node generates `{python} PrunedTree.b_str` extensions, the step validator rejects `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` of proposals, and the search proceeds to depth `{python} PrunedTree.depth_str`. The resulting effective branching factor is `{python} PrunedTree.b_eff_str`. For $\SearchBranchingFactor =$ `{python} PrunedTree.b_str` the critical rejection rate is `{python} PrunedTree.critical_prune_str`, and because the `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` rejection rate sits below it, the search remains supercritical ($\EffectiveBranchingFactor > 1$). An unpruned tree across these three steps generates `{python} PrunedTree.unpruned_generated_str` nodes and terminates with `{python} PrunedTree.unpruned_leaves_str` leaves. In contrast, the pruned search generates an expected `{python} PrunedTree.pruned_generated_str` nodes and retains approximately `{python} PrunedTree.pruned_leaves_str` leaves, eliminating `{python} PrunedTree.generated_saving_str` of total node generations. The aggregate reduction exceeds the raw `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` per-node rejection rate because pruning a single parent eliminates the entire combinatorial subtree beneath it. Assuming uniform step sizes, token generation savings follow the identical proportion, though each discarded node still incurs the upfront cost of its own generation and validation pass.

Two systems caveats govern this branching model. First, intermediate checks that exhibit false rejections irrevocably prune viable solution paths; aggressive pruning is therefore advantageous only when the validator's false-rejection rate remains tightly controlled. Second, consider a single step that needs only one surviving child to advance. Proposing children one at a time requires $1/(1 - \ChildPruningProbability)$ attempts in expectation. Proposing a batch of $\ChildBatchSize$ children in parallel requires $1/(1 - \ChildPruningProbability^{\,\ChildBatchSize})$ rounds instead, with each round generating $\ChildBatchSize$ children. Batching reduces elapsed wall-clock rounds at the expense of higher aggregate token expenditure, the same trade between concurrency and total work that notebook \ref{nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price} priced for best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling.

### Branch isolation {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-mutable-sandbox-search}

While a partial patch is an ephemeral candidate data structure, evaluating it requires concrete execution against a target environment. If one search branch mutates files in a shared workspace and a sibling branch subsequently runs against that modified working tree, the sibling's test outcomes no longer reflect its own proposed edits. A robust runtime must therefore isolate execution environments so that every observation binds strictly to the candidate patch and workspace snapshot that produced it. Stateful or mutating branches require independent execution containers, copy-on-write filesystem forks, or deterministic rollback procedures that restore a clean baseline before subsequent branches execute.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Copy-on-write task workspaces that keep each run's file modifications private are developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-cow-provisioning.
:::

Workspace isolation incurs substantial systems overhead even when a search branch is ultimately discarded. Concurrent sandboxes consume host memory, storage volumes, container daemon process slots, and network bandwidth, while their logged outputs accumulate in the agent's working context. Even read-only diagnostic commands require sandboxed execution permissions and can inadvertently leak environment variables or credentials into search traces. Pruning a candidate drops it from the active search frontier, but computational backtracking cannot undo remote side effects such as outbound network requests or database writes. Dedicated sandbox containment mechanisms enforce these operational boundaries, ensuring that search policies budget external actions under the reality that tree traversal cannot reverse real-world side effects.

### A resource ledger for the whole search {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-resource-ledger}

Managing search budgets requires maintaining separate ledgers for financial expenditure, physical work, wall-clock time, and live system state. Financial cost aggregates generator inferences, validation calls, and external tool invocations under a unified currency. Physical work dimensions, however, represent fundamentally non-interchangeable resource demands: generator prompt and completion tokens, scoring passes, unit test executions, and sandbox setup routines each stress different infrastructure bottlenecks. Summing hardware FLOPs with end-to-end test runtimes in seconds produces meaningless telemetry.

Elapsed wall-clock latency depends entirely on how execution scheduling maps these demands onto hardware. Sequential search phases sum latency along the critical path, parallel candidate evaluations overlap across available worker threads, and limited thread or accelerator allocations force excess requests into batched waves. Peak live state introduces yet another independent constraint. It reflects the maximum footprint held simultaneously in memory and storage (active KV caches, candidate ASTs, diagnostic logs, and running sandboxes) rather than the cumulative volume of candidates generated over the task lifetime. An optimization that reduces aggregate completion tokens often increases input token reprocessing, introduces synchronization barriers, or balloons memory occupancy. Tracking these dimensions in separate ledger accounts prevents composite cost metrics from masking critical systems bottlenecks.

```{python}
#| label: lego-bounded-search-ledger
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BOUNDED SEARCH RESOURCE LEDGER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search,
# │          nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs.
# │ Goal: Compare counted work, token charges, and scheduled time for two
# │       hypothetical policies without assigning either a quality advantage.
# │ Show: Expansion counts, input/output/scorer tokens, prices, and time.
# │ How: Registry-derived output allowance; explicit local workload, prices,
# │      concurrency, and nonoverlapping generation/scoring/test stages.
# │ Note: No prefix-reuse discount. Prefill and service overheads are omitted
# │       from the timing subtotal, not from generator input-token charges.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
from math import ceil

class SearchLedger:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    steps = 4  # hypothetical candidate length in equal-sized segments
    step_tokens = 128  # hypothetical newly generated tokens per extension
    prompt_tokens = 4096  # hypothetical common task prompt per request
    flat_candidates = 16  # hypothetical complete-candidate budget
    beam_width = 4  # hypothetical retained-prefix limit
    extensions = 3  # hypothetical extensions per retained prefix
    generation_slots = 8  # hypothetical concurrent streams, unchanged rate
    test_slots = 8  # hypothetical concurrent isolated test runs
    score_time = 15 * ms  # fixed scenario allowance per FULL-prefix score
    test_time = 0.5 * second  # fixed scenario allowance per final test
    price_in = 3 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical generator input rate
    price_out = 15 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical output rate
    price_score = 0.50 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical scorer input rate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * weight_bytes
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    retained = 1
    frontier_counts = []
    beam_prompt_tokens = 0
    scorer_tokens = 0
    beam_waves = 0
    for depth in range(1, steps + 1):
        expanded = retained * extensions
        frontier_counts.append(expanded)
        beam_prompt_tokens += expanded * (prompt_tokens + (depth - 1) * step_tokens)
        # The scorer reads each complete generated prefix, not only its suffix.
        scorer_tokens += expanded * depth * step_tokens
        beam_waves += ceil(expanded / generation_slots)
        retained = min(beam_width, expanded)
    beam_segments = sum(frontier_counts)
    beam_output_tokens = beam_segments * step_tokens
    flat_length = steps * step_tokens
    flat_output_tokens = flat_candidates * flat_length
    flat_prompt_tokens = flat_candidates * prompt_tokens
    flat_waves = ceil(flat_candidates / generation_slots)
    flat_test_waves = ceil(flat_candidates / test_slots)
    beam_test_waves = ceil(retained / test_slots)
    flat_generation_time = flat_waves * flat_length * token_time
    beam_generation_time = beam_waves * step_tokens * token_time
    beam_scoring_time = beam_segments * score_time
    flat_elapsed = flat_generation_time + flat_test_waves * test_time
    beam_elapsed = beam_generation_time + beam_scoring_time + beam_test_waves * test_time
    flat_token_cost = flat_prompt_tokens * count * price_in + flat_output_tokens * count * price_out
    beam_token_cost = beam_prompt_tokens * count * price_in + beam_output_tokens * count * price_out + scorer_tokens * count * price_score
    output_saving = 1 - beam_output_tokens / flat_output_tokens
    # Break-even: the input-price fraction (e.g. under prefix caching) at which
    # the beam's output saving net of scoring pays for its repeated input.
    out_saving_usd = ((flat_output_tokens - beam_output_tokens) * count * price_out).to(USD)
    scorer_usd = (scorer_tokens * count * price_score).to(USD)
    input_premium_usd = ((beam_prompt_tokens - flat_prompt_tokens) * count * price_in).to(USD)
    breakeven_input_share = ((out_saving_usd - scorer_usd) / input_premium_usd).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(frontier_counts == [3, 9, 12, 12], "Root expansion precedes a full beam")
    check(beam_segments == 36 and retained == 4, "Count extensions before pruning")
    check(flat_output_tokens == 8192 and beam_output_tokens == 4608, "Count generated suffixes once")
    check(scorer_tokens == 13440, "Full-prefix scoring rereads ancestor tokens")
    check(beam_prompt_tokens == 156288 and flat_prompt_tokens == 65536, "Bill every supplied prompt without reuse discount")
    check(beam_waves == 7 and flat_waves == 2, "Apply generation concurrency to each stage")
    check(abs(output_saving - 0.4375) < 1e-12, "Beam generates fewer output tokens in this scenario")
    check(beam_token_cost > flat_token_cost, "Repeated inputs reverse the token-charge ranking")
    check(0 < breakeven_input_share < 1, "Beam breaks even only at a discounted input price")
    check(22 * second < flat_elapsed < 23 * second, "Flat timing subtotal remains in its stated range")
    check(19 * second < beam_elapsed < 21 * second, "Beam timing subtotal remains in its stated range")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    steps_str = fmt_count(steps)
    step_tokens_str = fmt_count(step_tokens)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(prompt_tokens)
    flat_candidates_str = fmt_count(flat_candidates)
    beam_width_str = fmt_count(beam_width)
    extensions_str = fmt_count(extensions)
    generation_slots_str = fmt_count(generation_slots)
    test_slots_str = fmt_count(test_slots)
    token_time_ms_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit=ms, precision=3)
    score_time_ms_str = fmt_time(score_time, unit=ms, precision=0)
```
